Other preventive teaching includes exclusive breastfeeding, avoiding smoke exposure, and completing immunizations. Nothing should be inserted in an infant ear canal, since cotton buds push wax inward and can injure the canal. Memory aid: head higher than the stomach during every feed.

A is wrong: Bottle propping and sleeping with a bottle promote reflux into the ear.

C is wrong: Feeding flat raises the risk.

D is wrong: Cotton buds do not prevent middle ear infection.

105. Which finding helps the nurse tell otitis externa apart from otitis media?

A. Fever

B. A red, bulging eardrum

C. Pain increases when the pinna or tragus is pulled or pressed

D. A recent cold

Answer: C. Pain increases when the pinna or tragus is pulled or pressed

Otitis externa is inflammation or infection of the outer ear canal, so any movement of the pinna or pressure on the tragus stretches the inflamed canal skin and sharply increases pain. This is the classic bedside sign separating it from otitis media, where the infection sits behind the eardrum and pulling the ear does not hurt more. Also expect itching, canal swelling, and drainage in swimmer's ear. Fever, cold history, and a red bulging drum point to otitis media. Exam tip: tragus tenderness equals external ear problem.

A is wrong: Fever can occur in both.

B is wrong: A bulging eardrum is a sign of otitis media.

D is wrong: A recent cold usually comes before otitis media.

106. A client with dry AMD checks an Amsler grid daily at home. Which report needs prompt referral?

A. The grid looks the same as last week

B. Her eyes feel tired after reading for an hour

C. She needs her reading glasses for fine print

D. The lines suddenly look wavy and a new dark spot appears in the center

Answer: D. The lines suddenly look wavy and a new dark spot appears in the center

Dry age-related macular degeneration can convert to the wet form, in which abnormal fragile vessels leak and bleed under the macula. This causes sudden distortion, wavy lines on the Amsler grid, or a new central dark spot, and it needs urgent ophthalmologic treatment such as anti-VEGF injections to save central vision. Daily Amsler grid checking exists precisely to catch this change early. Stable findings, eye tiredness, and the need for reading glasses are common and not urgent. Priority rule: any sudden change in vision means prompt referral.

A is wrong: A stable grid shows no change.

B is wrong: Eye fatigue is not a sign of conversion.

C is wrong: Needing reading glasses is common and not urgent.

107. A construction worker in Taguig arrives at the clinic with a metal piece sticking out of his right eye. What should the nurse do?

A. Pull the object out quickly

B. Irrigate the eye forcefully

C. Apply a firm pressure patch over the eye

D. Stabilize the object and loosely cover both eyes without removing it

Answer: D. Stabilize the object and loosely cover both eyes without removing it

A penetrating foreign object in the eye must never be removed by the nurse, because pulling it out can cause bleeding and loss of vitreous or other eye contents. The object is stabilized, for example with a rigid shield or cup around it, and both eyes are loosely covered because the eyes move together and movement of the good eye moves the injured one. Avoid any pressure on the globe and avoid irrigation. Keep the client calm and still, and arrange immediate ophthalmology care. Memory aid: stabilize, cover both, do not remove, do not press.

A is wrong: Removal can cause bleeding and loss of eye contents.

B is wrong: Forceful irrigation can push contents out.

C is wrong: Pressure on the eye can push out its contents.

108. A client with hearing loss reads lips. Which action by the nurse is best when talking with him?

A. Shout into his better ear

B. Face him in good light and speak clearly at a normal pace

C. Talk while writing notes with her back to him

D. Exaggerate lip movements and speak very slowly

Answer: B. Face him in good light and speak clearly at a normal pace

A client who reads lips needs to see the speaker's face clearly, so the nurse stands in front in good light, keeps hands and objects away from the mouth, and speaks distinctly at a normal pace. Shouting distorts both sound and lip shape, and exaggerated mouth movements or very slow speech make lip patterns harder to recognize. Reduce background noise, get the client's attention before speaking, and rephrase instead of repeating the same words if not understood. Written notes or gestures can supplement but should not replace face-to-face speaking.

A is wrong: Shouting distorts sounds and lip shapes.

C is wrong: The client cannot read lips if the nurse looks away.

D is wrong: Exaggeration distorts lip shapes.

109. A client is suspected of having macular detachment from vitreomacular traction. Which diagnostic test does the nurse prepare the client for?

A. Gonioscopy

B. Tonometry

C. Optical coherence tomography

D. Perimetry

Answer: C. Optical coherence tomography

Optical coherence tomography uses light waves to produce cross-sectional images of the retina and macula, so it shows macular thickness, traction from the vitreous, holes, and detachment of the macular layers. It is painless and noninvasive, and the pupils may be dilated first. Compare it with other eye tests: tonometry measures intraocular pressure, gonioscopy inspects the drainage angle, and perimetry maps the visual field. Memory aid: OCT means optical cross-section of the retina. Nursing teaching includes explaining that no contact with the eye is needed and driving may be affected if dilating drops are used.

A is wrong: Gonioscopy views the anterior chamber angle.

B is wrong: Tonometry measures intraocular pressure.

D is wrong: Perimetry maps the visual field and is used mainly in glaucoma.

110. A nursing student asks which is the most common cause of vertigo. Based on the handout, the clinical instructor answers:

A. Head injury

B. Dental work

C. Prolonged lying on the back

D. Ear trauma

Answer: A. Head injury

The handout lists head injury as the most common cause of vertigo, along with ototoxic drugs, prolonged supine positioning, ear trauma, and dental work. Vertigo is the false sensation that the person or surroundings are spinning, and it arises from disturbance of the vestibular system in the inner ear, vestibular nerve, or brain. In many references, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is the most common single cause, and head trauma is a leading trigger of it, so answer according to the handout in this item. Nursing care includes fall precautions, slow position changes, and a quiet dim room during attacks.

B is wrong: Dental work is a less common cause.

C is wrong: Prolonged supine positioning is a less common cause.

D is wrong: Ear trauma is a less common cause.

111. During assessment of an 80-year-old client in a home for the aged in Quezon City, which finding is an expected change of aging?

A. A sudden curtain-like shadow over the vision

B. Increased sensitivity to glare and difficulty telling blue from green

C. Halos with severe eye pain and vomiting

D. A white reflex in the pupil

Answer: B. Increased sensitivity to glare and difficulty telling blue from green

Normal aging changes the lens and retina, causing sensitivity to glare, reduced night vision, and difficulty telling blue from green because the lens yellows. These are expected changes, so the nurse teaches safety measures such as sunglasses, good lighting, and caution with night driving. Danger signs differ: a curtain-like shadow suggests retinal detachment, halos with severe eye pain and vomiting suggest acute closed-angle glaucoma, and a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) is abnormal at any age. Exam tip: separate expected aging changes from emergency findings.

A is wrong: This suggests retinal detachment.

C is wrong: This suggests acute closed-angle glaucoma.

D is wrong: A white reflex is abnormal at any age.

112. A nursing student asks the nurse what happens in closed-angle glaucoma. The nurse correctly explains that:

A. The trabecular meshwork slowly clogs while the angle stays open

B. Proteins in the lens break down and make it cloudy

C. The iris bulges forward and blocks the drainage angle formed by the cornea and iris

D. Fluid collects between the layers of the retina

Answer: C. The iris bulges forward and blocks the drainage angle formed by the cornea and iris

In closed-angle glaucoma the iris bulges forward and blocks the angle between the cornea and iris, so aqueous humor cannot reach the trabecular meshwork and intraocular pressure rises abruptly. It is an emergency presenting with severe eye pain, halos around lights, blurred vision, nausea, vomiting, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. In contrast, open-angle glaucoma is slow, painless, and caused by gradual clogging of drainage. Treatment includes miotics, osmotic agents, and laser iridotomy. Memory aid: closed angle means acute and painful, open angle means chronic and silent.

A is wrong: This describes open-angle glaucoma.

B is wrong: This describes cataract.

D is wrong: This describes retinal detachment.

113. After a nosebleed is controlled at the barangay health station, which discharge instruction should the nurse give?

A. Blow the nose hard to clear the clots

B. Lift heavy objects to build strength

C. Avoid blowing or picking the nose, and do not take aspirin unless prescribed

D. Take aspirin for the nasal discomfort

Answer: C. Avoid blowing or picking the nose, and do not take aspirin unless prescribed

After epistaxis is controlled, the clot over the vessel is still fragile, so the client should avoid blowing or picking the nose, straining, heavy lifting, and bending down, and should not take aspirin or NSAIDs unless prescribed because they impair clotting. Teach to sneeze with the mouth open, keep the air moist, and use saline spray as advised. If bleeding recurs, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes. Remember never to tilt the head back, which makes blood run down the throat.

A is wrong: Forceful blowing can restart bleeding.

B is wrong: Straining raises pressure and bleeding risk.

D is wrong: Aspirin slows clotting.

114. A nursing student is instilling eye drops. Which action needs correction by the clinical instructor?

A. The dropper tip touches the client's lower eyelid

B. The student washes hands before the procedure

C. The student asks the client to look up

D. The student instills the drop into the lower conjunctival sac

Answer: A. The dropper tip touches the client's lower eyelid

Sterile technique requires that the dropper or tube tip never touches the eye, lashes, lids, or fingers, since contact contaminates the medication and spreads infection. The correct method is to wash hands, have the client look up, pull down the lower lid to form a conjunctival sac, and drop the medicine into the sac rather than directly on the cornea. Afterward the client closes the eyes gently without squeezing. When giving more than one drop type, wait about 5 minutes between them. The student touching the lid with the tip is the error.

B is wrong: Handwashing prevents contamination and is correct.

C is wrong: Looking up exposes the lower sac and is correct.

D is wrong: The lower conjunctival sac is the correct site.

115. A man feels a fish bone stuck in his throat after eating bangus. What should the nurse advise?

A. Swallow a ball of rice to push it down

B. Make yourself vomit

C. Go to the emergency room for removal and do not force down balls of rice

D. Drink vinegar to dissolve the bone

Answer: C. Go to the emergency room for removal and do not force down balls of rice

A fish bone lodged in the throat can be pushed deeper or can scratch or perforate the pharynx or esophagus if the client swallows rice balls, bread, or forces vomiting. The safe response is to stay calm, avoid forcing it down, and have it removed under direct vision by a physician, often with a laryngoscope or endoscope. Vinegar does not dissolve bones. Warn the client that pain, bleeding, or difficulty breathing makes it urgent. Memory aid: look and remove, never push down.

A is wrong: Rice balls can drive the bone deeper.

B is wrong: Vomiting can cause more injury.

D is wrong: Vinegar does not dissolve the bone and irritates the throat.

116. A housewife in Marikina gets sneezing fits and a runny nose every time she sweeps dust. What should the nurse recommend first for her allergic rhinitis?

A. Take antibiotics at the start of symptoms

B. Avoid or reduce exposure to dust

C. Have nasal packing inserted

D. Blow the nose forcefully every hour

Answer: B. Avoid or reduce exposure to dust

The first and most effective management for allergic rhinitis is avoiding or reducing contact with the trigger, such as dust, pollen, animal dander, or molds. Medicines like antihistamines, nasal steroids, and decongestants are added when avoidance is not enough. For dust allergy, teach damp dusting, washing bedding in hot water, wearing a mask while sweeping, and keeping the house well ventilated. The condition is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity, not an infection, so antibiotics have no role. Exam tip: identify the allergen, then avoid it.

A is wrong: Allergic rhinitis is not bacterial.

C is wrong: Nasal packing is for bleeding.

D is wrong: Forceful blowing irritates the nose.

117. The day after stapedectomy, a client is upset that his hearing is worse than before surgery. The nurse's best response is:

A. The surgery has failed

B. Hearing may be reduced at first because of packing and swelling and usually improves over the next weeks

C. The hearing loss is now permanent

D. Remove the ear packing yourself to hear better

Answer: B. Hearing may be reduced at first because of packing and swelling and usually improves over the next weeks

After stapedectomy the middle ear is filled with packing and the tissues are swollen, so hearing is temporarily poorer even if the operation succeeded. Hearing usually improves over several weeks as swelling resolves and the packing is absorbed or removed by the surgeon. The nurse reassures the client and also teaches to avoid blowing the nose, sneezing with a closed mouth, straining, and air travel, which could dislodge the prosthesis. Report severe vertigo, facial weakness, or drainage. Never remove the packing yourself.

A is wrong: Early hearing loss does not mean the surgery failed.

C is wrong: The decrease is usually temporary.

D is wrong: Only the surgeon removes the packing.

118. To screen an elderly client at a senior citizens' center for presbycusis, which question should the nurse ask?

A. Do you feel like the room is revolving?

B. Did you have a sore throat recently?

C. Do you have difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds?

D. Do you see halos around lights?

Answer: C. Do you have difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds?

Presbycusis is age-related sensorineural hearing loss that begins with high-pitched sounds and consonants such as s, f, and th, so the client hears speech but cannot understand it, especially in noisy rooms. Asking about difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds, ringing in the ears, and trouble following conversations helps detect it. It is bilateral and gradual. Communication tips include speaking in a lower pitch, facing the client, and reducing background noise. Memory aid: presbycusis means high pitch lost first.

A is wrong: This screens for vertigo.

B is wrong: This screens for streptococcal complications.

D is wrong: This screens for glaucoma or cataract.

119. A newly hired nurse in a Pampanga hospital asks which law requires hearing screening for all newborns in the Philippines. The charge nurse answers:

A. RA 9709, the Universal Newborn Hearing Screening and Intervention Act

B. RA 9288, the Newborn Screening Act of 2004

C. RA 10152, the Mandatory Infants and Children Health Immunization Act

D. RA 7600, the Rooming-In and Breastfeeding Act

Answer: A. RA 9709, the Universal Newborn Hearing Screening and Intervention Act

RA 9709, the Universal Newborn Hearing Screening and Intervention Act of 2009, requires hearing screening for all babies born in the Philippines, ideally before discharge or within the first 3 months of life, with intervention by 6 months. Early detection protects speech and language development. Distinguish it from the Newborn Screening Act (RA 9288) that covers metabolic disorders, from RA 10152 on immunization, and from RA 7600 on rooming-in and breastfeeding. Exam tip: match the law to its subject, hearing equals 9709, metabolic equals 9288.

B is wrong: RA 9288 covers screening for metabolic disorders.

C is wrong: RA 10152 covers basic immunization.

D is wrong: RA 7600 covers rooming-in and breastfeeding.

120. Which newborn in the NICU has an intra- or postnatal risk factor for hearing impairment?

A. A preterm newborn weighing 1,350 grams

B. A term newborn weighing 3,200 grams with mild jaundice that needed no treatment

C. A newborn with Apgar scores of 9 and 10

D. A breastfed newborn weighing 2,800 grams

Answer: A. A preterm newborn weighing 1,350 grams

A preterm newborn weighing 1,350 grams is below the 1,500 gram cutoff listed for very low birth weight, which is an intra- and postnatal risk factor for hearing impairment. Other risk factors include hyperbilirubinemia needing exchange transfusion, ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides, bacterial meningitis, severe asphyxia, prolonged ventilation, family history of deafness, and craniofacial anomalies. These infants need a hearing screen before discharge and follow-up testing. Normal weight with untreated mild jaundice and good Apgar scores does not carry the same risk.

B is wrong: Mild jaundice without exchange transfusion is not listed as a risk.

C is wrong: High Apgar scores show no asphyxia.

D is wrong: Normal weight and feeding are not risks.

121. A client with viral pharyngitis asks the nurse for antibiotics. The nurse's best response is:

A. Antibiotics do not work against viruses, but rest, fluids, lozenges and warm salt water gargles can ease your symptoms

B. Antibiotics will cure your viral infection in a day

C. Take your family member's leftover antibiotics

D. Do not drink fluids so your throat can rest

Answer: A. Antibiotics do not work against viruses, but rest, fluids, lozenges and warm salt water gargles can ease your symptoms

Viral pharyngitis is caused by viruses, so antibiotics do not shorten it and misuse promotes drug resistance. Comfort care includes rest, plenty of fluids, lozenges, warm salt water gargles, and over-the-counter analgesics or antipyretics. Antibiotics are reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection, where full treatment prevents rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. Teach the client to return if there is difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, or high fever. Never share or reuse leftover antibiotics.

B is wrong: Antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

C is wrong: Sharing leftover antibiotics is unsafe.

D is wrong: Fluids help soothe the throat and prevent dehydration.

122. Which child seen at a pediatric clinic in Quezon City is at greatest risk for developing amblyopia?

A. A 6-year-old with mild myopia in both eyes corrected with glasses

B. A 4-year-old with itchy allergic conjunctivitis

C. A 2-year-old with congenital ptosis that covers the pupil of one eye

D. A 3-year-old with a healed scratch on the eyelid skin

Answer: C. A 2-year-old with congenital ptosis that covers the pupil of one eye

Amblyopia (lazy eye) develops when one eye is deprived of clear, focused input during the critical period of visual development, so the brain suppresses that eye. A droopy lid covering the pupil blocks the image completely, which makes congenital ptosis a major risk, along with strabismus, anisometropia, and congenital cataract. Equal myopia in both eyes still gives each eye input, and allergic conjunctivitis or a healed skin scratch does not block vision. Early detection before about age 7 and prompt treatment offer the best outcome.

A is wrong: Equal, corrected myopia in both eyes does not deprive one eye.

B is wrong: Allergic conjunctivitis does not block vision.

D is wrong: A healed skin scratch does not affect visual input.

123. A call center agent in Makati has a painful, red, swollen lump at the edge of her upper eyelid diagnosed as a hordeolum (stye). Which instruction should the nurse give?

A. Squeeze the lump to drain the pus faster

B. Cover the lump with eye makeup until it heals

C. Rub the lump firmly with the fingers to break it up

D. Apply clean warm compresses to the eyelid several times a day

Answer: D. Apply clean warm compresses to the eyelid several times a day

A hordeolum (stye) is an acute bacterial, usually staphylococcal, infection of an eyelid gland or follicle. Warm compresses several times a day improve circulation and encourage the pus to drain on its own. Always wash hands first and use clean cloths. Never squeeze, rub, or puncture it because this can spread the infection into surrounding tissue, and avoid eye makeup and contact lenses until healed. Refer if it does not improve in a few days or if swelling spreads. Memory aid: warm, clean, hands off.

A is wrong: Squeezing can spread infection to surrounding tissue.

B is wrong: Makeup can contaminate the area and worsen infection.

C is wrong: Rubbing traumatizes the lid and spreads bacteria.

124. A 5-year-old is diagnosed with amblyopia. The ophthalmologist explains that one eye is nearsighted and the other is farsighted. The nurse recognizes this cause of amblyopia as:

A. Strabismus

B. Anisometropia

C. Ptosis

D. Nystagmus

Answer: B. Anisometropia

Anisometropia is a marked difference in refractive power between the two eyes, such as one nearsighted and the other farsighted. The brain favors the eye with clearer vision and suppresses the other, causing amblyopia. Compare with the other causes: strabismus is misalignment, ptosis is lid droop blocking the visual axis, and nystagmus is involuntary rhythmic eye movement. Treatment is corrective lenses and patching of the stronger eye, started early. Prefix memory aid: aniso means unequal, metropia means measure of vision.

A is wrong: Strabismus is misalignment of the eyes.

C is wrong: Ptosis is drooping of the eyelid.

D is wrong: Nystagmus is involuntary eye movement.

125. A 4-year-old pushed a mung bean (monggo) into his ear. Which action should the nurse avoid?

A. Referring the child for removal with proper instruments

B. Keeping the child calm and still

C. Looking at the canal with an otoscope

D. Irrigating the ear canal with water

Answer: D. Irrigating the ear canal with water

Vegetable matter such as a mung bean absorbs moisture and swells, so water irrigation makes it larger, tighter, and harder to remove, and it may also ferment. Irrigation is generally reserved for small inanimate objects that do not swell, and never when the eardrum may be perforated. The nurse keeps the child calm, inspects with an otoscope, and refers for removal by instruments. Do not poke with cotton buds or tweezers, which can push the object deeper. Insects, in contrast, are first immobilized with mineral oil.

A is wrong: Removal with instruments is appropriate.

B is wrong: Keeping the child still prevents injury.

C is wrong: Inspection is appropriate.

126. The nurse teaches a client with tonsillitis to prepare a salt water gargle. The correct mixture is:

A. Half teaspoon of table salt in 1 glass of water

B. 2 tablespoons of salt in half a glass of water

C. Half teaspoon of salt in 1 liter of water

D. 1 cup of salt in 1 glass of water

Answer: A. Half teaspoon of table salt in 1 glass of water

A standard salt water gargle uses about half a teaspoon of table salt in one glass (about 240 mL) of warm water. This isotonic-like strength soothes inflamed tissues and loosens mucus, while too much salt dries and irritates the throat and too little gives no benefit. The client may gargle several times a day and spit, not swallow. This is a comfort measure used with rest, fluids, and lozenges, and does not replace antibiotics when a bacterial cause such as strep is confirmed. Persistent pain or fever needs medical review.

B is wrong: Too much salt irritates the throat.

C is wrong: Too dilute to be helpful.

D is wrong: Far too concentrated.

127. A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant comes to a lying-in clinic in Bulacan with blurred vision and headache. Her BP is 150/100 mmHg. The nurse suspects:

A. A normal visual change of pregnancy

B. Pregnancy-induced hypertension

C. New-onset myopia

D. Cataract formation

Answer: B. Pregnancy-induced hypertension

Blurred vision, headache, and a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg at 32 weeks signal pregnancy-induced hypertension, which can progress to severe preeclampsia and eclampsia. Visual disturbances, severe headache, epigastric pain, and hyperreflexia show central nervous system irritation and are warning signs needing urgent evaluation. Expect to check urine protein, edema, and reflexes, and prepare for magnesium sulfate if ordered. Priority teaching: report these symptoms immediately and do not wait. Antidote note for magnesium sulfate is calcium gluconate.

A is wrong: Blurred vision with high BP is not normal.

C is wrong: Myopia does not cause headache and high BP.

D is wrong: Cataract does not explain the high BP.

128. Which statement by a client after retinal detachment repair shows correct understanding of discharge teaching?

A. Flashes of light are expected and do not need to be reported

B. I can lift my sack of rice tomorrow

C. I will rub my eye gently if it itches

D. I will report a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light or a curtain over my vision

Answer: D. I will report a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light or a curtain over my vision

After retinal detachment repair, signs such as new floaters, flashes of light, or a curtain-like shadow mean the retina may be detaching again and need immediate reporting. Activities that raise intraocular pressure or strain the operated eye are avoided, including heavy lifting, rubbing the eye, bending with the head down, and straining at stool. Teach correct eye drop use, shield at night, and maintaining the prescribed head position, especially when a gas bubble is used. Memory aid: floaters, flashes, and a curtain mean call right away.

A is wrong: Flashes may signal another detachment.

B is wrong: Heavy lifting raises intraocular pressure.

C is wrong: Rubbing can injure the operated eye.

129. A client asks the nurse how a chalazion differs from a stye. The most accurate response is that a chalazion is:

A. A painful acute bacterial infection of an eyelash follicle

B. Usually a painless lump caused by a blocked oil gland of the eyelid

C. An inward turning of the edge of the eyelid

D. An infection of the cornea

Answer: B. Usually a painless lump caused by a blocked oil gland of the eyelid

A chalazion is a chronic, usually painless, slow-growing lump caused by a blocked meibomian (oil) gland deeper in the eyelid. A stye is acute, tender, and infected at the lid margin. Chalazia often resolve with warm compresses and lid hygiene, and persistent ones may need incision and curettage. Entropion is an inward-turned lid and keratitis is corneal infection, so they are unrelated. Memory aid: stye is sore and superficial, chalazion is chronic and painless.

A is wrong: This describes a stye or hordeolum.

C is wrong: This describes entropion.

D is wrong: Infection of the cornea is keratitis.

130. Which statement by a client about hearing aid care needs further teaching?

A. I will wash my hearing aid in soapy water every night

B. I will remove the battery when I am not using it

C. I will wipe it with a soft dry cloth

D. I will turn it off before taking it out

Answer: A. I will wash my hearing aid in soapy water every night

Hearing aids contain delicate electronics, so water, soap, and moisture can ruin them. Proper care includes wiping with a soft dry cloth, cleaning the ear mold as the manufacturer directs, turning the aid off and removing the battery when not in use, and storing it in a dry place away from heat. Turning it off before removal prevents high-pitched feedback. Teach to replace batteries regularly and keep spare ones. A client who washes the aid in soapy water needs further teaching.

B is wrong: Removing the battery saves power and is correct.

C is wrong: Wiping with a dry cloth is correct.

D is wrong: Turning it off before removal prevents feedback.

131. A client with otosclerosis asks whether her dizzy spells are related to her ear problem. The nurse's best response is:

A. Yes, vertigo occurs in as many as 30 percent of clients with otosclerosis

B. No, otosclerosis never causes dizziness

C. Dizziness means you have meningitis

D. Every client with otosclerosis has vertigo

Answer: A. Yes, vertigo occurs in as many as 30 percent of clients with otosclerosis

Otosclerosis is abnormal bone growth that fixes the stapes in the oval window, causing progressive conductive hearing loss, and it may also produce tinnitus and vertigo from inner ear involvement. About 30 percent of clients report vertigo, so dizziness is not unusual, but not every client has it. The nurse reassures her, advises fall precautions, and explains treatment options such as stapedectomy or hearing aids. Dizziness here does not suggest meningitis. Exam tip: otosclerosis means conductive loss, worse in the young adult woman, and is often hereditary.

B is wrong: Otosclerosis can cause vertigo.

C is wrong: Meningitis is not suggested by these findings.

D is wrong: Vertigo affects up to 30 percent, not all.

132. While assessing a rice farmer from Nueva Ecija who complains of a scratchy eye, the nurse sees several eyelashes growing inward and rubbing against the cornea while the lid margin is in normal position. The nurse documents this as:

A. Ectropion

B. Ptosis

C. Trichiasis

D. Chalazion

Answer: C. Trichiasis

Trichiasis is the inward growth of eyelashes that rub against the cornea, causing scratchiness, tearing, redness, and risk of corneal abrasion or ulcer, while the lid margin itself remains in normal position. In entropion the whole lid margin turns inward, and in ectropion the lower lid turns outward. Treatment includes epilation of the lashes, electrolysis, or cryotherapy for recurrent cases. Memory aid: trich means hair, so trichiasis is a hair problem. Teach the client not to rub the eye and to seek care to protect the cornea.

A is wrong: Ectropion is an outward turning of the lower lid.

B is wrong: Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid.

D is wrong: A chalazion is a lump at the lid from a blocked gland.

133. A 10-year-old had an untreated sore throat 3 weeks ago and now has fever, painful joints and a new heart murmur. The nurse suspects:

A. Rheumatic fever, which can lead to mitral valve stenosis

B. Acute glomerulonephritis

C. Epiglottitis

D. Otitis media

Answer: A. Rheumatic fever, which can lead to mitral valve stenosis

Untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis can lead to rheumatic fever 2 to 4 weeks later, producing fever, migratory joint pain, and carditis with a new murmur, most often affecting the mitral valve and later causing mitral stenosis. Diagnosis uses the Jones criteria, and treatment includes penicillin, anti-inflammatory drugs, and rest. Glomerulonephritis also follows strep infection but presents with edema, hematuria, and hypertension. Prevention is full antibiotic treatment of every strep throat and secondary prophylaxis with penicillin. Memory aid: strep throat then joints and heart.

B is wrong: AGN presents with edema, hematuria and hypertension.

C is wrong: Epiglottitis causes airway distress and drooling.

D is wrong: Otitis media causes ear pain.

134. A tricycle driver using pilocarpine eye drops says he has trouble seeing when driving at night. The nurse explains that:

A. The drug dilates the pupil and causes glare

B. This is a sign of retinal detachment

C. The drug is raising his eye pressure

D. The drug constricts the pupil, so less light enters the eye in dim conditions

Answer: D. The drug constricts the pupil, so less light enters the eye in dim conditions

Pilocarpine is a miotic that constricts the pupil and contracts the ciliary muscle to improve aqueous outflow in glaucoma. A small pupil lets in less light, so dim lighting and night vision become difficult, which is an expected side effect and a safety issue for a tricycle driver. Teach to avoid night driving and hazardous tasks until vision adapts, to use good lighting at home, and to report severe eye pain or sudden vision change. Antidote and opposite drugs are mydriatics like atropine.

A is wrong: Pilocarpine constricts, not dilates, the pupil.

B is wrong: Night vision difficulty is an expected miotic effect.

C is wrong: Pilocarpine lowers eye pressure.

135. A nurse is caring for two infants: one after cleft lip repair and one after cleft palate repair. Which positioning is correct?

A. The cleft lip infant prone and the cleft palate infant supine

B. Both infants prone

C. Both infants supine

D. The cleft lip infant supine and the cleft palate infant prone

Answer: D. The cleft lip infant supine and the cleft palate infant prone

After cleft lip repair, the infant is placed supine or on the side so that the delicate suture line is not rubbed against the mattress, and arm restraints may be used to prevent touching. After cleft palate repair, prone positioning allows secretions and blood to drain from the mouth and prevents aspiration. Mnemonic: lip stays up and palate goes down. Also keep the airway clear, feed with the prescribed device, avoid hard objects in the mouth, and clean the suture line as ordered.

A is wrong: This reverses the correct positions.

B is wrong: Prone positioning can rub the repaired lip.

C is wrong: Supine positioning can cause aspiration after palate repair.

136. A client with suspected open-angle glaucoma is scheduled for perimetry. The nurse explains that this test:

A. Measures the pressure inside the eye

B. Examines the drainage angle with a special lens

C. Maps the visual field to detect loss of side vision

D. Compares air and bone conduction

Answer: C. Maps the visual field to detect loss of side vision

Perimetry maps the visual field, and in glaucoma the loss typically starts at the periphery and progresses inward, causing tunnel vision. It is therefore a key test to detect and monitor the disease. Tonometry measures intraocular pressure (normal about 10 to 21 mmHg), and gonioscopy examines the drainage angle to tell open from closed type. The Rinne test compares air and bone conduction for hearing. The nurse explains that the client must look straight ahead and press a button when lights appear in the side vision.

A is wrong: This describes tonometry.

B is wrong: This describes gonioscopy.

D is wrong: This describes the Rinne test.

137. A 3-year-old has had foul-smelling, pus-like discharge from only one nostril for a week. The nurse suspects:

A. Allergic rhinitis

B. A foreign body in the nose

C. Common cold

D. Epiglottitis

Answer: B. A foreign body in the nose

A foul-smelling, purulent discharge from only one nostril in a young child strongly suggests a foreign body, such as a bead, bean, or paper, retained in the nose. Allergic rhinitis and colds affect both sides, and discharge in allergy is clear and watery. The child should be referred for removal, and the parents taught not to try digging it out or to let the child sniff hard, which can push the object back toward the airway. Prevention includes keeping small objects away from children.

A is wrong: Allergic rhinitis usually causes clear discharge from both nostrils.

C is wrong: A cold usually affects both nostrils.

D is wrong: Epiglottitis affects the airway, not the nose.

138. A 58-year-old smoker has been hoarse for 5 weeks. Which diagnostic procedure does the nurse anticipate?

A. A lateral neck X-ray only

B. Throat lozenges and watching for 6 months

C. Tonometry

D. Laryngoscopy, with biopsy if needed

Answer: D. Laryngoscopy, with biopsy if needed

Hoarseness lasting more than 2 to 3 weeks in an older smoker is considered cancer of the larynx until proven otherwise. Laryngoscopy gives direct or indirect viewing of the vocal cords, and biopsy of suspicious lesions confirms the diagnosis. Waiting or giving lozenges only delays treatment, and plain X-rays cannot show vocal cord lesions. Other risk factors are heavy alcohol use and chronic irritant exposure. Teach smoking cessation and prompt evaluation. Memory aid: hoarse for more than 2 weeks needs a look.

A is wrong: An X-ray cannot show vocal cord lesions well.

B is wrong: Waiting delays diagnosis of possible cancer.

C is wrong: Tonometry measures eye pressure.

139. A 15-year-old is hit in the eye by a basketball. Blood is layered in the front of the eye, and a hyphema is diagnosed. How should the nurse position him?

A. Flat on the back

B. Bed rest with the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees

C. In Trendelenburg position

D. Prone with the face down

Answer: B. Bed rest with the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees

A hyphema is bleeding into the anterior chamber, and the client is placed on bed rest with the head of the bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees so blood settles at the bottom of the chamber and clears the pupil. This also helps lower intraocular pressure and promote reabsorption. Avoid straining, bending, and aspirin or NSAIDs, which may cause rebleeding, and use an eye shield. Watch for rising pain or pressure. Lying flat, Trendelenburg, or prone positions spread blood and raise pressure.

A is wrong: Lying flat spreads blood over the visual axis.

C is wrong: Head-down positions raise eye pressure.

D is wrong: Prone positioning does not let blood settle properly.

140. Which discharge teaching is correct for a client with a permanent laryngectomy stoma?

A. Swim to strengthen the lungs

B. Keep the stoma uncovered in dusty places

C. Use powder on the skin around the stoma

D. Cover the stoma with a shower shield when bathing and do not swim

Answer: D. Cover the stoma with a shower shield when bathing and do not swim

After laryngectomy the stoma leads directly to the trachea and lungs, so water, dust, powder, and food particles entering it can cause aspiration or infection. The client should use a shower shield or hold the water stream away when bathing, avoid swimming, cover the stoma with a loose bib or scarf to filter and warm air, and avoid powders and aerosols. Humidify the home air and clean the stoma daily. Memory aid: stoma is a direct line to the lungs, keep it dry and covered.

A is wrong: Swimming risks aspiration and drowning.

B is wrong: The stoma should be covered to filter dust.

C is wrong: Powder can be inhaled through the stoma.

141. A newly admitted client at a provincial hospital is registered as legally blind. When planning care, the nurse remembers that the majority of visually impaired persons:

A. Have total absence of light perception

B. Cannot be oriented to their surroundings

C. Have some residual vision such as light, color or form perception

D. Must communicate only through braille

Answer: C. Have some residual vision such as light, color or form perception

Most clients classified as legally blind still have some residual vision, such as perception of light, color, or form, so care should maximize what remains through good lighting, contrast, and large print. They can learn to orient to surroundings with verbal cues and touch, and braille is only one of many communication methods, along with audio recordings and assistive technology. Total blindness with no light perception is much less common. Promote independence and always explain what is happening.

A is wrong: Total blindness without light perception is the minority.

B is wrong: Visually impaired clients can be oriented verbally and by touch.

D is wrong: Many use large print, recordings or residual vision, not only braille.

142. After instilling ear drops, the nurse places a cotton ball loosely in the outer ear. The client asks why. The nurse explains that it:

A. Keeps excess medicine from dripping out and does not reduce absorption

B. Absorbs extra medicine to prevent overdose

C. Warms the drops to body temperature

D. Blocks sound so the ear can rest

Answer: A. Keeps excess medicine from dripping out and does not reduce absorption

A cotton ball placed loosely in the outer ear after ear drops keeps the medicine from dripping out, and it does not reduce the absorption of the drug into the canal. It must be placed loosely and never pushed into the canal. Instill drops at body temperature to avoid vertigo, and in adults pull the pinna up and back while in children under 3 years pull it down and back. Keep the client lying on the side for about 5 minutes afterward for the medicine to spread.

B is wrong: Its purpose is not to prevent overdose.

C is wrong: Drops should be warmed before instillation.

D is wrong: It is not meant to block hearing.

143. When reviewing a 10-year-old's history, which item should the nurse note as a late-onset risk factor for hearing impairment?

A. One episode of the common cold last month

B. Head trauma with loss of consciousness after a motorcycle accident

C. Mild seasonal allergies

D. Tonsillectomy last year

Answer: B. Head trauma with loss of consciousness after a motorcycle accident

Head trauma with loss of consciousness or skull fracture is a late-onset, acquired risk factor for hearing impairment because injury can damage the temporal bone, ossicles, or inner ear. Other late-onset factors include meningitis, ototoxic drugs, noise, and recurrent otitis media. A simple cold, mild allergy, or tonsillectomy is not on the list. The nurse documents the history, refers for audiology testing, and educates on helmet use during motorcycle riding. Prevention of head injury is part of preventing hearing loss.

A is wrong: A single cold is not a listed risk.

C is wrong: Mild allergies are not a listed risk.

D is wrong: Tonsillectomy is not a listed risk.

144. During Garantisadong Pambata week in a barangay, a mother says her 3-year-old cannot see well at dusk. The nurse suspects a deficiency of:

A. Vitamin C

B. Iron

C. Vitamin A

D. Vitamin D

Answer: C. Vitamin A

Vitamin A is needed for the retinal pigment that works in dim light, so night blindness is an early sign of deficiency, followed by xerophthalmia and Bitot spots. During Garantisadong Pambata, vitamin A capsules are given to children 6 to 59 months old, 100,000 IU for ages 6 to 11 months and 200,000 IU for ages 12 to 59 months. Teach to include yellow and green leafy vegetables, liver, and eggs. Vitamin C deficiency gives scurvy, iron gives anemia, and vitamin D gives rickets.

A is wrong: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

B is wrong: Iron deficiency causes anemia.

D is wrong: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.

145. A 3-year-old with newly fitted hearing aids still has delayed speech. Which referral should the nurse make?

A. Optometrist

B. Registered dietitian

C. Speech-language pathologist

D. Ophthalmologist

Answer: C. Speech-language pathologist

A speech-language pathologist assesses and treats delays in speech and language, and works with children who have hearing loss to develop communication even after hearing aids are fitted. Hearing aids alone do not guarantee speech development, so early therapy with the family is important. The audiologist handles hearing testing and fitting, the optometrist and ophthalmologist handle vision, and the dietitian handles nutrition. Exam tip: match each member of the EENT team to the problem, speech and language delays go to the speech-language pathologist.

A is wrong: Optometrists manage vision.

B is wrong: Dietitians manage nutrition.

D is wrong: Ophthalmologists manage eye disease.

146. Which finding is most consistent with acute bacterial sinusitis?

A. Clear, watery discharge with sneezing during allergy season

B. A painless lump on the eyelid

C. Drooling and a muffled voice in a 4-year-old

D. Facial pain and pressure that worsen when bending forward, with thick discolored nasal discharge

Answer: D. Facial pain and pressure that worsen when bending forward, with thick discolored nasal discharge

Acute bacterial sinusitis causes facial pain or pressure over the affected sinuses, which worsens when bending forward, along with thick purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and sometimes fever and a toothache. Allergic rhinitis gives clear watery discharge and sneezing, a chalazion is a painless eyelid lump, and epiglottitis causes drooling and a muffled voice. Management includes antibiotics, decongestants, steam inhalation, warm compresses, and fluids. Report severe headache, swelling around the eyes, or vision change, which may mean spread of infection.

A is wrong: This suggests allergic rhinitis.

B is wrong: This suggests a chalazion.

C is wrong: This suggests epiglottitis.

147. Which glaucoma medication is a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces aqueous humor production?

A. Dorzolamide

B. Netarsudil

C. Travoprost

D. Carbachol

Answer: A. Dorzolamide

Dorzolamide is a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that lowers intraocular pressure by reducing the production of aqueous humor. Compare with other glaucoma classes: prostaglandin analogs such as travoprost increase outflow, miotics such as pilocarpine and carbachol open outflow by contracting the pupil, beta blockers such as timolol reduce production, and rho kinase inhibitors such as netarsudil improve trabecular outflow. Teach that the drops may sting and give a bitter taste, and sulfa allergy is a caution. Memory aid: zolamide means carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.

B is wrong: Netarsudil is a rho kinase inhibitor.

C is wrong: Travoprost is a prostaglandin analog that increases outflow.

D is wrong: Carbachol is a miotic.

148. A jeepney driver's Snellen test result for license renewal is 20/40 in each eye. The nurse explains that this means:

A. He reads at 20 feet what a person with normal vision reads at 40 feet

B. He reads at 40 feet what a normal person reads at 20 feet

C. He has lost 40 percent of his vision

D. He is legally blind

Answer: A. He reads at 20 feet what a person with normal vision reads at 40 feet

In Snellen notation the top number is the testing distance, usually 20 feet, and the bottom number is the distance at which a person with normal vision can read the same line. A result of 20/40 means the client must be at 20 feet to read what a normal eye reads at 40 feet, so his vision is poorer than normal. The fractions are not percentages, and legal blindness is defined as 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction. A larger bottom number means worse vision. Refer for refraction if below 20/20 with symptoms.

B is wrong: This reverses the meaning of the numbers.

C is wrong: Snellen fractions are not percentages.

D is wrong: Legal blindness is 20/200 or worse.

149. A client with Meniere's disease is prescribed acetazolamide (Diamox). Which finding shows the drug is effective?

A. Fewer episodes of vertigo

B. Decreased urine output

C. Improved near vision

D. Dilated pupils

Answer: A. Fewer episodes of vertigo

Acetazolamide (Diamox) is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and diuretic that reduces the fluid pressure in the inner ear, so effectiveness is shown by fewer and milder vertigo attacks and by increased urine output. The nurse also monitors electrolytes, especially potassium, because of the diuretic effect, and teaches a low-sodium diet as part of the treatment. Report numbness or tingling, rash, or unusual bleeding. Treatment of Meniere's disease aims to control vertigo, tinnitus, and fluid imbalance, since there is no cure.

B is wrong: Urine output increases with this diuretic.

C is wrong: Near vision is not the treatment goal.

D is wrong: Acetazolamide does not dilate the pupils.

150. A 68-year-old grandmother and her 6-month-old grandchild both have constantly watery eyes. The grandmother asks if this is unusual. The nurse explains that epiphora:

A. Always means bacterial conjunctivitis requiring contact precautions

B. Only occurs in clients with glaucoma

C. Is common among babies below 12 months and adults above 60 years

D. Is caused by the eyes producing no tears at all

Answer: C. Is common among babies below 12 months and adults above 60 years

Epiphora is excessive tearing caused by overproduction of tears or by blocked drainage, such as a blocked nasolacrimal duct. It is common in babies under 12 months because the duct is still developing, and in adults over 60 because of lid laxity and reduced drainage. It has many causes, including infection, allergy, and irritation, so it is not specific to glaucoma or conjunctivitis. Management in infants includes gentle massage of the tear sac, and most clear by 12 months. Report if redness, pus, or fever develops.

A is wrong: Watery eyes have many causes besides bacterial infection.

B is wrong: Epiphora is not limited to glaucoma.

D is wrong: Epiphora is excess tearing, not absence of tears.

151. Which discharge instruction about light and driving is correct for a client after eye surgery?

A. Wear sunglasses outdoors, use brighter lamps indoors and limit night driving

B. Keep the rooms dim at home

C. Avoid sunglasses so the eye adjusts faster

D. Practice driving at night to regain confidence

Answer: A. Wear sunglasses outdoors, use brighter lamps indoors and limit night driving

After eye surgery the eyes are sensitive to light and glare, so the client wears sunglasses outdoors, uses brighter lamps indoors to see better, and limits night driving until the doctor allows it. Dim rooms increase fall risk, and removing sunglasses causes discomfort. Other discharge teaching includes using shields at night, avoiding rubbing, lifting, and bending, and taking eye drops as directed. Report severe pain, sudden vision loss, or discharge. Safety and protection are the focus of recovery.

B is wrong: Dim rooms increase the risk of falls.

C is wrong: Sunglasses protect against glare.

D is wrong: Night driving should be limited.

152. A client with nasal polyps and asthma is being prepared for polypectomy. Which history is most important to report?

A. Taking acetaminophen for headaches

B. Taking vitamin C daily

C. Wheezing episodes after taking aspirin

D. Using an antacid after meals

Answer: C. Wheezing episodes after taking aspirin

Nasal polyps with asthma and sensitivity to aspirin form Samter's triad, in which even a small dose of aspirin or other NSAIDs can trigger severe bronchospasm. The nurse reports a history of wheezing after aspirin so that these drugs are avoided before and after polypectomy. Polyps are soft swellings of the nasal lining that obstruct breathing, reduce smell, and may recur. Acetaminophen is generally a safer alternative. Exam tip: aspirin plus asthma plus polyps equals a dangerous triad, always ask about drug allergies.

A is wrong: Acetaminophen is not linked to this reaction.

B is wrong: Vitamin C is not significant here.

D is wrong: Antacid use is not significant here.

153. Which client has the greatest risk for laryngeal cancer?

A. A 25-year-old woman who sings in a church choir

B. A 60-year-old man who smokes two packs a day and drinks heavily

C. A 30-year-old teacher with seasonal allergies

D. A 40-year-old nonsmoker who drinks a lot of water

Answer: B. A 60-year-old man who smokes two packs a day and drinks heavily

Tobacco smoking and heavy alcohol use are the main risk factors for laryngeal cancer, and the combination multiplies the risk, especially in men over 50. Voice overuse, allergies, and low water intake are not major causes. Warning signs include persistent hoarseness over 2 to 3 weeks, sore throat, dysphagia, ear pain, and a neck mass. Teach smoking cessation and limiting alcohol, and refer early for laryngoscopy. Early detection greatly improves cure rates.

A is wrong: Voice use alone is not a major cancer risk.

C is wrong: Allergies are not a cancer risk.

D is wrong: This client has no major risk factors.

154. A pregnant woman had rubella during her first trimester. Which ear-related problem does the nurse anticipate in the newborn?

A. Otitis externa

B. Sensorineural hearing impairment

C. Impacted cerumen

D. Otosclerosis

Answer: B. Sensorineural hearing impairment

Maternal rubella in the first trimester is one of the intrauterine TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, other, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) that damage the developing cochlea and cause sensorineural hearing loss, and may also cause cataract and congenital heart defects. The newborn needs a hearing screen under RA 9709 and early intervention. Otitis externa and cerumen impaction affect the outer ear, and otosclerosis is a middle ear bone disease. Prevention includes rubella immunization before pregnancy, which is a live vaccine and is avoided during pregnancy.

A is wrong: Otitis externa is an outer ear canal infection.

C is wrong: Cerumen impaction is not related to rubella.

D is wrong: Otosclerosis is abnormal bone growth in the middle ear.

155. A client with Meniere's disease has an acute attack of vertigo. Which anti-motion sickness drug does the nurse anticipate based on the handout?

A. Pilocarpine

B. Diazepam

C. Timolol

D. Phenylephrine

Answer: B. Diazepam

Diazepam, a benzodiazepine, is used to suppress vestibular activity and reduce the spinning sensation and anxiety during an acute Meniere's attack, along with antiemetics such as meclizine, diuretics, and sometimes steroids. Pilocarpine, timolol, and phenylephrine are eye drugs for glaucoma and mydriasis. Teach the client to lie down in a quiet place during an attack, avoid sudden head movement, and observe safety because diazepam causes drowsiness. Avoid alcohol and driving while taking it.

A is wrong: Pilocarpine is a miotic for glaucoma.

C is wrong: Timolol is a beta blocker for glaucoma.

D is wrong: Phenylephrine is a mydriatic.

156. A client with Meniere's disease that is not controlled by other treatments is scheduled for middle ear gentamicin injections. The nurse explains that the purpose is to:

A. Treat a bacterial infection of the inner ear

B. Reduce the balance function of the affected ear to control vertigo

C. Improve hearing in the affected ear

D. Dry up secretions in the middle ear

Answer: B. Reduce the balance function of the affected ear to control vertigo

Middle ear gentamicin is a chemical labyrinthectomy because gentamicin is vestibulotoxic, so it reduces the balance function of the diseased ear and relieves vertigo when other treatments fail. The risk is possible hearing loss, so hearing is monitored, and it is not given to treat infection. After the procedure the client may feel unsteady for a few days and needs fall precautions. Meniere's disease is caused by excess endolymph, and the usual first steps are diet changes and diuretics.

A is wrong: Meniere's disease is not a bacterial infection.

C is wrong: Gentamicin may worsen, not improve, hearing.

D is wrong: Drying secretions is not the purpose.

157. Which lifestyle teaching should the nurse give a client with Meniere's disease, in addition to a low-sodium diet?

A. Drink three cups of strong coffee daily

B. Eat salty chicharon as a snack

C. Drink alcohol to relax the inner ear

D. Limit caffeine and alcohol, and stop smoking

Answer: D. Limit caffeine and alcohol, and stop smoking

Caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine can worsen fluid imbalance and constrict inner ear vessels, which may provoke vertigo and tinnitus in Meniere's disease. Along with a low-sodium diet, the client should limit these, stop smoking, manage stress, get adequate rest, and avoid sudden position changes. Salty foods such as chicharon increase fluid retention in the endolymphatic space. Teach fall precautions and not to drive during attacks. Dietary and lifestyle control reduces how often attacks happen.

A is wrong: Caffeine can worsen symptoms.

B is wrong: Salty foods worsen fluid buildup.

C is wrong: Alcohol can trigger attacks.

158. A child is treated for retinoblastoma in both eyes, and the parents are planning another pregnancy. Which member of the multidisciplinary team should the nurse refer them to?

A. Audiologist

B. Geneticist

C. Speech-language pathologist

D. Optometrist

Answer: B. Geneticist

Bilateral retinoblastoma is usually hereditary, caused by a mutation in the RB1 gene, so there is a high chance of passing it to future children and affected family members need screening. A geneticist offers risk assessment and counseling and helps the parents make informed reproductive decisions. The audiologist, speech-language pathologist, and optometrist have different roles in hearing, speech, and refraction. Nursing role includes supporting the family and ensuring that any new child gets early eye examinations.

A is wrong: Audiologists manage hearing.

C is wrong: Speech-language pathologists manage speech and language.

D is wrong: Optometrists manage refractive and early vision problems.

159. A child with untreated otitis media now has pain, redness and swelling behind the ear, and the ear is pushed forward. The nurse suspects:

A. Mastoiditis

B. Otitis externa

C. Otosclerosis

D. Meniere's disease

Answer: A. Mastoiditis

Mastoiditis is infection of the mastoid air cells behind the ear, usually from untreated or inadequately treated otitis media. Signs include pain, redness, tenderness, and swelling behind the ear that pushes the pinna forward and outward, with fever and discharge. It needs IV antibiotics and may need surgery, because spread can cause meningitis or brain abscess. Prevention is complete treatment of every ear infection. Otitis externa and otosclerosis do not show mastoid swelling, and Meniere's disease presents with vertigo and tinnitus.

B is wrong: Otitis externa affects the ear canal.

C is wrong: Otosclerosis is abnormal bone growth without signs of infection.

D is wrong: Meniere's disease causes vertigo and tinnitus.

160. Which NICU intervention helps prevent retinopathy of prematurity in a 29-week preterm newborn?

A. Give 100 percent oxygen continuously to all preterm newborns

B. Keep the incubator lights very bright

C. Adjust oxygen to keep oxygen saturation within the ordered target range and avoid too much oxygen

D. Delay the first eye examination until 1 year of age

Answer: C. Adjust oxygen to keep oxygen saturation within the ordered target range and avoid too much oxygen

In preterm infants the retinal vessels are not fully developed, and too much oxygen causes abnormal vessel growth that can lead to retinal detachment and blindness (retinopathy of prematurity). The nurse titrates oxygen to keep saturation within the ordered target range, uses blended oxygen, monitors with pulse oximetry, and ensures timely eye screening, usually 4 to 6 weeks after birth or by 31 weeks postmenstrual age, for infants born at 30 weeks or earlier or weighing under 1,500 grams. Oxygen is a drug, so give the lowest effective dose.

A is wrong: Too much oxygen increases the risk of ROP.

B is wrong: Bright light does not prevent ROP.

D is wrong: Screening must be done early so treatment is not missed.

161. The nurse teaches a client how to use a corticosteroid nasal spray. Which instruction is correct?

A. Aim the spray directly at the nasal septum

B. Aim the spray away from the nasal septum toward the outer side of the nostril

C. Blow the nose right after spraying

D. Sniff hard so the drug goes to the throat and swallow it

Answer: B. Aim the spray away from the nasal septum toward the outer side of the nostril

The correct nasal spray technique is to aim the nozzle away from the septum, toward the outer wall of the nostril, because spraying the septum irritates it and may cause bleeding or perforation. Shake the bottle, blow the nose gently first, keep the head upright, and sniff gently, not hard. Do not blow the nose right after spraying, since this removes the drug. Report nosebleeds, and remember that steroid sprays take several days for full effect, so teach regular use.

A is wrong: Spraying at the septum can cause bleeding and damage.

C is wrong: Blowing removes the drug.

D is wrong: The drug should stay in the nose, not be swallowed.

162. A client with suspected bacterial keratitis from overnight contact lens wear calls the clinic. What is the nurse's priority instruction?

A. Keep wearing the lenses but clean them twice a day

B. Remove the lenses, do not wear them again, and see the ophthalmologist today

C. Use leftover steroid eye drops from a previous illness

D. Rinse the lenses with tap water and reinsert them

Answer: B. Remove the lenses, do not wear them again, and see the ophthalmologist today

Overnight contact lens wear is a major risk factor for bacterial keratitis, and corneal infection can quickly cause ulceration, scarring, and permanent vision loss. The priority instruction is to remove the lenses, avoid wearing them again, and be examined by an ophthalmologist the same day. Never use leftover steroid drops, which may worsen infection, and never rinse lenses with tap water, which can carry Acanthamoeba. Teach to follow the wearing schedule, replace lenses and cases, and wash hands before handling them.

A is wrong: Continued wear worsens the infection.

C is wrong: Unprescribed steroids can worsen a corneal infection.

D is wrong: Tap water can carry organisms such as Acanthamoeba.

163. A client asks how he will breathe after his total laryngectomy. The nurse explains:

A. You will breathe permanently through the stoma in your neck

B. You will breathe through your nose once you heal

C. You will breathe through your mouth

D. The tube is temporary and will be removed in a week

Answer: A. You will breathe permanently through the stoma in your neck

In total laryngectomy the larynx is removed and the trachea is brought to the neck as a permanent tracheostomy, so the airway is separated from the mouth and nose. The client breathes only through the stoma and loses the ability to smell and to speak naturally. Teach stoma care, humidification, and alternative communication such as esophageal speech, an electrolarynx, or a tracheoesophageal puncture. Promoting body image and coping is also part of the care plan.

B is wrong: Air no longer passes through the nose.

C is wrong: Air no longer passes through the mouth.

D is wrong: The stoma is permanent.

164. A client is prescribed apraclonidine eye drops for glaucoma. The nurse explains that this alpha-adrenergic agonist lowers eye pressure by:

A. Constricting the pupil only

B. Reducing aqueous humor production and increasing its outflow

C. Dilating the pupil and constricting blood vessels

D. Suppressing rho kinase enzymes

Answer: B. Reducing aqueous humor production and increasing its outflow

Apraclonidine is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humor production and increasing its outflow. This is different from miotics that constrict the pupil, mydriatics that dilate it, and rho kinase inhibitors such as netarsudil that act on the trabecular meshwork. Teach about common effects such as eye redness and dry mouth, and use pressure on the inner canthus after instillation to limit systemic absorption. Glaucoma drugs are used lifelong to control pressure.

A is wrong: Pupil constriction is the action of miotics.

C is wrong: Pupil dilation is the action of mydriatics.

D is wrong: This is the action of netarsudil.

165. A 20-year-old has a severe one-sided sore throat, difficulty opening his mouth, a muffled voice and a uvula pushed to one side. The nurse suspects:

A. Laryngitis

B. Allergic rhinitis

C. Otitis externa

D. Peritonsillar abscess

Answer: D. Peritonsillar abscess

A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the throat wall, usually a complication of tonsillitis. Typical findings are severe one-sided sore throat, trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), muffled hot-potato voice, drooling, fever, and a uvula pushed toward the opposite side. Treatment includes needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus IV antibiotics. Watch the airway. Laryngitis causes hoarseness, allergic rhinitis involves the nose, and otitis externa involves the canal.

A is wrong: Laryngitis causes hoarseness without trismus.

B is wrong: Allergic rhinitis affects the nose.

C is wrong: Otitis externa affects the ear canal.

166. A 55-year-old client in Iloilo with type 2 diabetes asks what he can do to keep diabetic retinopathy from getting worse. The nurse's best teaching is to:

A. Wear dark sunglasses at all times

B. Use pilocarpine eye drops daily

C. Take large doses of vitamin A

D. Keep his blood sugar and blood pressure within target levels

Answer: D. Keep his blood sugar and blood pressure within target levels

Diabetic retinopathy results from long-term damage to the tiny retinal blood vessels by high blood glucose and high blood pressure. The best way to slow it is to keep blood sugar, blood pressure, and lipids within target levels, along with yearly dilated eye examinations and not smoking. Sunglasses do not protect the vessels, pilocarpine treats glaucoma, and large vitamin A doses can be toxic. Laser treatment or anti-VEGF injections are used for advanced disease. Exam tip: control the diabetes to protect the eyes.

A is wrong: Sunglasses do not protect retinal vessels.

B is wrong: Pilocarpine is for glaucoma.

C is wrong: Vitamin A megadoses do not prevent retinopathy and can be toxic.

167. A client taking high-dose aspirin for arthritis says she hears ringing in both ears. What should the nurse do?

A. Reassure her that this is a harmless side effect

B. Give the next dose with milk

C. Instill warm oil into both ears

D. Hold the next dose and report it as a possible sign of salicylate toxicity

Answer: D. Hold the next dose and report it as a possible sign of salicylate toxicity

Ringing in the ears (tinnitus) after high-dose aspirin is an early sign of salicylate toxicity, which can progress to hearing loss, nausea, and confusion. The nurse holds the next dose and reports to the physician so the dose can be adjusted. It should not be dismissed as a harmless side effect. Giving the drug with milk helps the stomach but does not prevent ototoxicity, and ear drops do not treat the cause. Also monitor for bleeding and respiratory changes. Other ototoxic drugs include aminoglycosides and loop diuretics.

A is wrong: Tinnitus here may signal toxicity.

B is wrong: Milk does not prevent ototoxicity.

C is wrong: Ear drops do not treat drug toxicity.

168. A farmer comes to the rural health unit saying a live insect is buzzing inside his ear. What is the nurse's initial action?

A. Insert a cotton bud to pull the insect out

B. Irrigate the ear with hot water

C. Instill mineral oil into the ear to kill the insect before removal

D. Have him lie on that ear until the insect crawls out

Answer: C. Instill mineral oil into the ear to kill the insect before removal

For a live insect in the ear canal, the first step is to instill mineral oil (or lidocaine as ordered), which kills and immobilizes the insect and stops the distressing buzzing, and then remove it by irrigation or instruments. Cotton buds can push it deeper, hot water can burn the canal and eardrum, and lying on that ear traps the insect. Contrast this with vegetable foreign bodies, which are not irrigated because they swell. Keep the client calm and refer if removal fails.

A is wrong: A cotton bud can push the insect deeper or injure the canal.

B is wrong: Hot water can burn the canal and eardrum.

D is wrong: Lying on the ear traps the insect.

169. Right after a total laryngectomy, what is the nurse's priority?

A. Teach esophageal speech

B. Start oral feedings

C. Assess body image concerns

D. Keep the airway open by suctioning secretions through the laryngectomy tube as needed

Answer: D. Keep the airway open by suctioning secretions through the laryngectomy tube as needed

Immediately after total laryngectomy, airway patency comes first because swelling and thick secretions can block the stoma or tube. The nurse suctions as needed using sterile technique, positions in semi-Fowler's, provides humidified air, and monitors breathing and oxygen saturation. Body image, speech rehabilitation, and oral feeding are important but come later, since feeding is delayed to protect the suture line and begins by tube first. Remember the priority rule: airway, breathing, circulation.

A is wrong: Speech training comes later.

B is wrong: Oral feeding is delayed to protect the suture line.

C is wrong: Body image matters but comes after airway.

170. Which IV antibiotic does the nurse anticipate for a child with epiglottitis based on the handout?

A. Ceftriaxone

B. Acyclovir

C. Metronidazole

D. Isoniazid

Answer: A. Ceftriaxone

Epiglottitis is usually caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, so treatment includes IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or ampicillin-sulbactam, with airway protection and corticosteroids as ordered. Acyclovir is an antiviral, metronidazole is for anaerobes and protozoa, and isoniazid treats tuberculosis. The nurse keeps intubation or tracheostomy equipment ready and keeps the child calm. Signs are the 4 Ds: drooling, dysphagia, dysphonia, and distress. Never examine the throat with a tongue depressor.

B is wrong: Acyclovir is an antiviral.

C is wrong: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and protozoa.

D is wrong: Isoniazid treats tuberculosis.

171. A 70-year-old client who lost an eye to trauma wears an ocular prosthesis. He asks the nurse at a Pasig clinic how to clean it at home. The nurse instructs him to clean it with:

A. Plain water

B. 70 percent isopropyl alcohol soaked overnight

C. An abrasive powder to remove deposits

D. Hydrogen peroxide poured directly into the socket

Answer: A. Plain water

An artificial eye (ocular prosthesis) is cleaned with plain water or mild soap and water, rinsed well, and dried gently. Alcohol, abrasives, and harsh chemicals scratch the surface and irritate the socket. Teach the client to wash hands first, hold the prosthesis over a soft towel or basin to prevent damage if dropped, and report redness, discharge, or pain in the socket. Regular checks with the ocularist are also needed because the fit changes over time.

B is wrong: Alcohol can damage the prosthesis surface and irritate the socket.

C is wrong: Abrasives scratch the prosthesis and irritate tissue.

D is wrong: Peroxide in the socket irritates the tissue and is not the recommended cleaning agent.

172. The nurse is preparing communication aids on a surgical ward. For which client is a communication board most appropriate?

A. A client with presbycusis who reads lips well

B. A client who cannot speak after a total laryngectomy

C. A client with myopia corrected with eyeglasses

D. A client with tinnitus who hears normal speech

Answer: B. A client who cannot speak after a total laryngectomy

A communication board uses letters, words, or pictures that the client points to, so it is most useful when the person cannot speak but can see, read, or understand. After total laryngectomy the natural voice is lost, so a communication board, pad and pencil, or electronic device is provided early. Clients with presbycusis or tinnitus can still speak, and corrected myopia does not affect communication. Plan the aid before surgery and teach the client and family how to use it.

A is wrong: Lip reading and facing the client meet this client's needs.

C is wrong: Corrected myopia does not affect communication.

D is wrong: This client can hear and speak normally.

173. A nursing aide is assigned to a client who is totally blind. Which action by the aide upon entering the room is correct?

A. Touches the client's shoulder first without speaking

B. Speaks loudly because blind clients also hear poorly

C. Says her name and the purpose of the visit before doing anything

D. Rearranges the client's personal items to tidy the room

Answer: C. Says her name and the purpose of the visit before doing anything

A totally blind client should be told who is entering and why before being touched or helped, since he cannot see the person approach. Speak in a normal tone, because blindness does not mean hearing loss, and keep personal items and furniture in the same place so he can find them. Describe the room layout and offer an arm when walking, allowing him to hold the elbow. Always explain what you are doing before doing it. Avoid sudden touch or silent entry.

A is wrong: Touching without warning startles a blind client.

B is wrong: Blindness does not imply hearing loss.

D is wrong: Moving items makes them hard for the client to find.

174. After vitrectomy with a gas bubble for retinal detachment, which discharge instruction is a priority?

A. Lie flat on the back at all times

B. Keep the prescribed head position and avoid air travel until the gas is absorbed

C. Fly home to the province the day after surgery

D. Bend over to wash the hair on the first day

Answer: B. Keep the prescribed head position and avoid air travel until the gas is absorbed

After vitrectomy with a gas bubble, the client must hold the prescribed head position, often face down, so the bubble presses against the retinal break and seals it. Air travel, high altitude, and nitrous oxide anesthesia must be avoided until the gas is absorbed, because the bubble expands as pressure drops and can cause a dangerous rise in intraocular pressure and vision loss. Clients often wear a wristband stating gas in the eye. Also avoid bending, lifting, and straining, and report severe pain or sudden vision decrease.

A is wrong: The position must place the bubble against the break, often face down.

C is wrong: Altitude changes expand the gas bubble.

D is wrong: Bending raises intraocular pressure.

175. While waiting for the airway team, a 3-year-old with suspected epiglottitis sits on his mother's lap, leaning forward. What should the nurse do?

A. Keep him on his mother's lap in the position he prefers and keep him calm

B. Lay him flat to examine him

C. Take him from his mother so an IV can be started first

D. Swab his throat for culture

Answer: A. Keep him on his mother's lap in the position he prefers and keep him calm

In suspected epiglottitis, anything that distresses the child can trigger complete airway obstruction, so the child stays in the tripod or forward-leaning position of comfort, preferably on the parent's lap, and is kept calm. Do not lay him flat, examine the throat with a spatula, take a throat culture, or begin painful procedures before the airway is secured. Give oxygen by blow-by if tolerated and prepare intubation or tracheostomy equipment, with the team at the bedside. Remember the 4 Ds: drooling, dysphagia, dysphonia, distress.

B is wrong: Lying flat can block the airway.

C is wrong: Separation and painful procedures cause crying and can block the airway.

D is wrong: The handout warns against throat culture or inspection.

176. A client has posterior nasal packing for severe epistaxis. Which assessment is the priority?

A. Sense of smell

B. Bowel sounds

C. Breathing and oxygen saturation, since the packing can block the airway

D. Visual acuity

Answer: C. Breathing and oxygen saturation, since the packing can block the airway

Posterior nasal packing can slip backward and obstruct the airway, and it can also cause hypoxia or reflex bradycardia, so airway and breathing are the priority assessment. Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and any swallowing of blood, and keep scissors or a cutting tool for emergency removal as per hospital protocol. Other care includes bed rest in semi-Fowler's, mouth care, humidified oxygen, and watching for bleeding and infection. The ABC priority applies: airway first.

A is wrong: Smell is reduced anyway and is not the priority.

B is wrong: Bowel sounds are not related to this risk.

D is wrong: Visual acuity is not related to this risk.

177. A child is receiving atropine eye drops. Which instruction should the nurse give the parents?

A. Avoid tasks that need sharp vision and avoid hot environments

B. Expect a slow heart rate

C. Expect the pupils to become very small

D. Encourage active play under the noon sun

Answer: A. Avoid tasks that need sharp vision and avoid hot environments

Atropine eye drops dilate the pupil (mydriasis) and paralyze accommodation (cycloplegia), causing blurred near vision and light sensitivity. Atropine also reduces sweating, so hot environments increase the risk of heat intolerance and fever. Teach parents to avoid tasks needing acute vision and to avoid hot places, to wear sunglasses, and to watch for systemic effects such as flushing, fever, and tachycardia. Press on the inner canthus after instilling the drops to reduce absorption.

B is wrong: Atropine causes tachycardia.

C is wrong: Atropine dilates the pupils.

D is wrong: Heat and bright sun are poorly tolerated.

178. After instilling timolol drops, the nurse presses gently on the inner corner of the client's eye for 1 to 2 minutes. The purpose is to:

A. Spread the drug over the cornea

B. Stimulate tear production

C. Reduce systemic absorption of the drug through the tear duct

D. Prevent dilation of the pupil

Answer: C. Reduce systemic absorption of the drug through the tear duct

Pressing on the nasolacrimal duct at the inner corner of the eye for 1 to 2 minutes after drops keeps the medicine from draining into the nose and being absorbed systemically. This is particularly important for timolol, a beta blocker that can cause bradycardia, hypotension, and bronchospasm, so it is used with caution in clients with asthma, COPD, or heart block. Teach the client to close the eyes gently after instilling drops and not blink repeatedly. This simple technique also increases the time the medicine is in contact with the eye.

A is wrong: Blinking, not pressure on the duct, spreads the drug.

B is wrong: Pressure does not stimulate tears.

D is wrong: Timolol does not dilate the pupil.

179. A worker at a Valenzuela factory splashes an alkaline cleaning solution into both eyes. What is the nurse's first action?

A. Neutralize the chemical with vinegar

B. Patch both eyes and transport him to the hospital

C. Flush the eyes right away with plenty of clean water or saline for at least 15 minutes

D. Check visual acuity before doing anything else

Answer: C. Flush the eyes right away with plenty of clean water or saline for at least 15 minutes

Chemical burns of the eye are emergencies, so the first action is immediate, copious irrigation with water or saline for at least 15 minutes, starting at the scene before transport. Alkali burns are especially dangerous because they penetrate deeply and continue damaging tissue, so delay costs vision. Do not try to neutralize the chemical, since this may cause a second reaction, and do not patch the eyes before flushing. Irrigate from the inner to the outer canthus away from the unaffected eye, then check acuity and refer.

A is wrong: Neutralizing agents cause more chemical injury.

B is wrong: Patching delays irrigation and traps the chemical.

D is wrong: Irrigation takes priority over acuity testing.
