180. An 82-year-old client in a Laguna nursing home has a lower eyelid whose edge turns in toward the eye, so the lashes scrape the eyeball and the eye is red and teary. The nurse recognizes this condition as:

A. Ectropion

B. Exotropia

C. Hordeolum

D. Entropion

Answer: D. Entropion

Entropion is the turning inward of the lid margin, which brings the lashes against the cornea, and it is common in the elderly because of weakened lid muscles. Symptoms are redness, tearing, foreign body sensation, and risk of corneal ulcer. Ectropion is the opposite, with the lid turning outward, exotropia is a type of strabismus involving the eyeball, and hordeolum is a lump. Treatment includes lubricants, taping, and surgical correction. Memory aid: entropion means in, ectropion means out.

A is wrong: Ectropion is the lid turning outward and downward.

B is wrong: Exotropia is an outward deviation of the eyeball itself.

C is wrong: A hordeolum is a painful lump at the lid margin.

181. The ophthalmologist orders patching for a 4-year-old with amblyopia of the left eye. The nurse teaches the mother to patch:

A. The weaker left eye so it can rest

B. Both eyes alternately every hour

C. The left eye only while the child sleeps

D. The stronger right eye so that the weaker left eye is forced to work

Answer: D. The stronger right eye so that the weaker left eye is forced to work

Occlusion therapy for amblyopia means patching the stronger eye so that the weaker eye is forced to work and its visual pathways develop. Covering the weak eye worsens the condition, and patching only during sleep gives no stimulation. The patch is worn for several hours daily as prescribed, with activities that require close vision. Teach the parents about the importance of compliance, skin care under the patch, and regular follow-up. Best results occur when treatment starts before about age 7.

A is wrong: Covering the weak eye worsens amblyopia.

B is wrong: Alternate hourly patching of both eyes is not the standard treatment.

C is wrong: Patching during sleep gives no visual stimulation.

182. A college student who sleeps with her contact lenses on reports eye pain, redness, tearing, light sensitivity and blurred vision. The ophthalmologist diagnoses an infection of the cornea. The nurse records this as:

A. Conjunctivitis

B. Blepharitis

C. Dacryocystitis

D. Keratitis

Answer: D. Keratitis

Keratitis is inflammation or infection of the cornea, and extended wear of contact lenses is a major risk factor. Symptoms include pain, redness, tearing, photophobia, and blurred vision, and untreated cases cause corneal ulcers and scarring. Conjunctivitis affects the conjunctiva and gives discharge with less pain, blepharitis involves the lid margins, and dacryocystitis involves the tear sac. Management includes stopping lens wear and giving prescribed antimicrobial drops. Memory aid: kerato means cornea.

A is wrong: Conjunctivitis involves the conjunctiva, not the cornea.

B is wrong: Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins.

C is wrong: Dacryocystitis is infection of the tear sac.

183. A client with conjunctivitis has crusted discharge and old ointment on the eyelids. Before applying the next dose of eye ointment, the nurse should first:

A. Apply the new ointment over the old one

B. Clean from the outer to the inner canthus

C. Remove the old ointment and drainage, cleaning from the inner to the outer canthus

D. Rinse the eye with the client's ear drops

Answer: C. Remove the old ointment and drainage, cleaning from the inner to the outer canthus

Before applying new eye ointment, the nurse removes any old ointment and crusted drainage by wiping gently from the inner canthus to the outer canthus with clean, moistened gauze. This prevents debris from entering the tear duct or the other eye, and allows the new drug to contact the conjunctiva. Use a new swab for each wipe, wash hands first, and apply ointment in a thin line along the lower conjunctival sac from inner to outer corner. Use only products meant for the eye.

A is wrong: Old ointment and drainage block contact with the eye.

B is wrong: Outer to inner moves debris toward the tear duct.

D is wrong: Otic preparations must never be used in the eye.

184. A client with open-angle glaucoma tells the nurse, 'Once my eye pressure is normal, I can stop my eye drops.' The nurse's best response is:

A. Yes, you may stop once your pressure is normal

B. Use the drops only when you have eye pain

C. Using the drops regularly will bring back the vision you lost

D. Glaucoma has no cure, so the drops must be used for life to keep the pressure controlled

Answer: D. Glaucoma has no cure, so the drops must be used for life to keep the pressure controlled

Open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, painless condition that cannot be cured, and drops control intraocular pressure only while they are used. Stopping them lets pressure rise again and damage the optic nerve, and vision already lost cannot be restored. The nurse teaches lifelong adherence, regular follow-up, pressure checks, and visual field tests. Since there is no pain to signal a problem, relying on symptoms is unsafe. Emphasize that drops prevent further loss and not restore sight.

A is wrong: Pressure rises again when drops are stopped.

B is wrong: Open-angle glaucoma is usually painless, so pain is not a guide.

C is wrong: Optic nerve damage from glaucoma is permanent.

185. After repeated phenylephrine (Neo-Synephrine) eye drops before cataract surgery, which finding should the nurse report?

A. Dilated pupil

B. Mild, temporary blurring of vision

C. Brief stinging on instillation

D. Palpitations with an irregular heart rhythm

Answer: D. Palpitations with an irregular heart rhythm

Phenylephrine is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that dilates the pupil, but with repeated use it can be absorbed and cause systemic sympathetic effects such as hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, and dysrhythmias. Palpitations and an irregular rhythm need prompt reporting. Expected local effects include pupil dilation, temporary blurred vision, and brief stinging. Use press on the inner canthus to reduce absorption, and use caution in clients with heart disease or hypertension. Monitor vital signs.

A is wrong: Pupil dilation is the intended effect.

B is wrong: Temporary blurring is expected after mydriatics.

C is wrong: Brief stinging is minor and expected.

186. Which client is a candidate for a cochlear implant?

A. A child with profound sensorineural hearing loss in both ears who is not helped by hearing aids

B. A client with conductive hearing loss from impacted cerumen

C. A child with otitis media with effusion

D. A client with otosclerosis that improved after stapedectomy

Answer: A. A child with profound sensorineural hearing loss in both ears who is not helped by hearing aids

A cochlear implant is considered for children and adults with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss who get little or no benefit from hearing aids. It bypasses the damaged hair cells and stimulates the auditory nerve directly through electrodes in the cochlea. Conductive problems such as cerumen impaction, otitis media with effusion, and otosclerosis are treated by removal, tubes, or stapedectomy. Early implantation helps speech development, and the child needs intensive auditory training after surgery.

B is wrong: Cerumen is removed, not treated with an implant.

C is wrong: Otitis media is treated medically or with tubes.

D is wrong: Otosclerosis is conductive loss treated surgically.

187. A student with strep throat started on antibiotics asks when she may go back to school. The nurse's best response is:

A. Right away, since strep throat is not contagious

B. After at least 24 hours of antibiotics and when she no longer has a fever

C. Only after 2 full weeks at home

D. Only after three negative throat cultures

Answer: B. After at least 24 hours of antibiotics and when she no longer has a fever

Strep throat is spread by droplets, and a client is generally no longer contagious after at least 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy and when the fever is gone. The child can then return to school, but the full course of antibiotics, usually 10 days of penicillin, must still be completed to prevent rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. Teach to replace the toothbrush after treatment, cover coughs, and handwashing. Repeated cultures are not required for return.

A is wrong: Strep throat spreads by droplets.

C is wrong: Two weeks of isolation is unnecessary.

D is wrong: Repeated cultures are not needed to return to school.

188. A father asks if it is too late to correct the nearsightedness that was only discovered in his 12-year-old son. The nurse's best response is:

A. It can only be corrected if found before age 5

B. It will always lead to permanent amblyopia at this age

C. It can only be corrected with surgery

D. Refractive errors such as myopia can be corrected regardless of the child's age when detected

Answer: D. Refractive errors such as myopia can be corrected regardless of the child's age when detected

Refractive errors such as myopia and hyperopia that are not associated with amblyopia can be corrected by eyeglasses or contact lenses at any age, so it is never too late for a 12-year-old. In contrast, amblyopia must be treated early, ideally before about age 7, because the visual brain pathways lose plasticity. Vision screening in school helps find these problems, and uncorrected myopia can affect learning. Reassure the father and arrange an eye examination and prescription.

A is wrong: There is no age cutoff for correcting myopia.

B is wrong: Myopia not associated with amblyopia does not automatically cause it.

C is wrong: Eyeglasses or contact lenses usually correct myopia.

189. A client lost his voice after singing karaoke all night at a fiesta. Which instruction should the nurse give for his laryngitis?

A. Whisper instead of talking

B. Clear the throat often

C. Rest the voice and avoid whispering, which also strains the vocal cords

D. Keep singing to stretch the vocal cords

Answer: C. Rest the voice and avoid whispering, which also strains the vocal cords

Laryngitis is inflammation of the larynx, often from voice overuse, infection, or irritants, and the vocal cords need complete rest to heal. Whispering strains the cords even more than normal speech, so the client should avoid both talking and whispering, avoid throat clearing, smoking, and alcohol, and use humidified air and plenty of fluids. Voice rest may be needed for a few days. Report hoarseness beyond 2 weeks or breathing difficulty. Memory aid: rest means silence, not whispering.

A is wrong: Whispering strains the cords.

B is wrong: Throat clearing irritates the larynx.

D is wrong: More singing worsens the inflammation.

190. Which instruction should the nurse give after tonsillectomy?

A. Gargle hard with mouthwash every hour

B. Drink fluids through a straw

C. Avoid coughing, clearing the throat, gargling hard and using straws

D. Clear the throat often to remove mucus

Answer: C. Avoid coughing, clearing the throat, gargling hard and using straws

After tonsillectomy, the operative site is raw and clots protect it, so the client must avoid coughing, throat clearing, vigorous gargling, and using straws, which create suction or force that can dislodge the clot and cause hemorrhage. Offer cool clear fluids and soft, bland foods, avoid red or brown liquids that can hide blood, and avoid acidic, spicy, and hot foods. Watch for frequent swallowing, which signals bleeding. Position on the side or semi-prone until awake to keep the airway clear.

A is wrong: Vigorous gargling can cause bleeding.

B is wrong: Straw suction can dislodge clots.

D is wrong: Throat clearing raises bleeding risk.

191. A client has used an oxymetazoline nasal spray every day for 3 weeks, and his congestion is now worse. The nurse explains that this is most likely:

A. A sign that the dose should be doubled

B. Allergic rhinitis that has turned into pneumonia

C. An expected and harmless effect

D. Rebound congestion from overuse, so the spray should be limited to 3 to 5 days

Answer: D. Rebound congestion from overuse, so the spray should be limited to 3 to 5 days

Prolonged use of topical decongestants like oxymetazoline causes rebound congestion, called rhinitis medicamentosa, as the blood vessels become dependent on the drug. Use should be limited to no more than 3 to 5 days, and the client should stop the spray and may use saline or a nasal steroid under medical advice. Doubling the dose makes it worse. Explain that this is a preventable adverse effect and not an infection such as pneumonia. Teach reading medication labels and not to share sprays.

A is wrong: More spray worsens rebound congestion.

B is wrong: Rebound congestion is not pneumonia.

C is wrong: It is a preventable adverse effect.

192. During a well-baby visit, the nurse notes that a 1-year-old's pupil looks grayish instead of black. What should the nurse do?

A. Reassure the mother that this is normal for age

B. Refer the child promptly to an ophthalmologist

C. Recheck the eye when the child is 5 years old

D. Apply warm compresses to the eye

Answer: B. Refer the child promptly to an ophthalmologist

A grayish or white pupil in a child, called leukocoria, is abnormal and may indicate congenital cataract, retinoblastoma, or other serious disease. It needs prompt referral to an ophthalmologist, since delay can cost vision, cause amblyopia, or in the case of retinoblastoma, threaten life. Reassurance and waiting are inappropriate, and warm compresses do not treat lens or retinal problems. The red reflex test during newborn and infant checkups helps detect this early. Memory aid: white reflex means refer right away.

A is wrong: A grayish pupil is not normal in children.

C is wrong: Waiting risks permanent vision loss and amblyopia.

D is wrong: Warm compresses do not treat lens or retinal disease.

193. Right after delivery in a lying-in clinic, which eye care does the nurse give to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum?

A. Irrigate the eyes with tap water

B. Instill atropine eye drops

C. Instill erythromycin eye ointment into each lower conjunctival sac

D. Patch both eyes for 24 hours

Answer: C. Instill erythromycin eye ointment into each lower conjunctival sac

Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis in the newborn caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis acquired during passage through the birth canal. Prophylaxis is erythromycin 0.5 percent ophthalmic ointment (or as stated in the facility protocol) placed in the lower conjunctival sac of each eye, from the inner to the outer canthus, within the first hour after birth. The tip must not touch the eye. Do not wipe it off immediately, and delay is allowed briefly to promote bonding. This is part of essential newborn care.

A is wrong: Tap water is not sterile and does not prevent infection.

B is wrong: Atropine dilates the pupil and has no antibacterial effect.

D is wrong: Patching interferes with bonding and does not prevent infection.

194. A 70-year-old asks how phacoemulsification will remove his cataract. The nurse explains that:

A. Ultrasound breaks up the cloudy lens, which is then suctioned out through a small incision

B. A laser reshapes the cornea

C. Eye drops dissolve the cataract over several weeks

D. A freezing probe forms a scar inside the eye

Answer: A. Ultrasound breaks up the cloudy lens, which is then suctioned out through a small incision

Phacoemulsification uses ultrasound energy to break up the clouded lens (cataract), which is then suctioned out through a small incision, followed by insertion of an intraocular lens. Surgery is the only effective treatment for cataract, and no drops or medicines dissolve it. It is usually done as outpatient surgery with local anesthesia and gives quick recovery. Corneal reshaping is refractive surgery, and freezing is cryotherapy used for retinal tears. After surgery, teach to wear a shield, avoid rubbing and heavy lifting, and report pain or vision loss.

B is wrong: Corneal reshaping is refractive surgery, not cataract removal.

C is wrong: No eye drops dissolve cataracts.

D is wrong: Freezing describes cryopexy for retinal tears.

195. During a school health assessment in Malabon, the nurse notes that a 9-year-old's eyes move involuntarily from side to side while he reads. The teacher asks how to help him in class. The nurse's best suggestion is:

A. Give him extra time for reading so he can scan the text

B. Seat him at the very back of the room to reduce eye strain

C. Ask him to read faster so his eyes do not get tired

D. Keep one eye patched during all classes

Answer: A. Give him extra time for reading so he can scan the text

The child shows nystagmus, which is involuntary, rhythmic eye movement that can reduce visual acuity and make reading slow and tiring. Giving extra time to read and scan text, good lighting, large print, and seating near the board are helpful accommodations. Seating at the back, rushing, or patching one eye does not help, since patching is for amblyopia. The nurse coordinates with the teacher and refers for ophthalmologic evaluation. Support self-esteem and avoid pressure to read fast.

B is wrong: Sitting farther away makes print harder to see.

C is wrong: Rushing worsens comprehension and does not control the eye movement.

D is wrong: Patching is for amblyopia, not nystagmus.

196. A client taking acetazolamide (Diamox) for glaucoma asks about safety precautions while on the drug. Which instruction is appropriate?

A. Drive as usual because the drug has no effect on alertness

B. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and report any unusual bleeding

C. Expect a decrease in urine output

D. Sunbathe daily to prevent drowsiness

Answer: B. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and report any unusual bleeding

Acetazolamide is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that can cause drowsiness, dizziness, photosensitivity, and rarely blood disorders, so the client should avoid driving or hazardous tasks until response is known, avoid prolonged sun exposure, and report unusual bleeding, bruising, sore throat, or rash. It increases urine output and may cause low potassium and a tingling sensation in the fingers. Report severe symptoms. Teach to take it with food and keep up fluid intake. Caution in sulfa allergy.

A is wrong: The handout advises avoiding driving.

C is wrong: Acetazolamide increases urine output.

D is wrong: Sun exposure should be avoided.

197. A welder reports a scratchy, painful eye after working without goggles. Which test does the nurse anticipate to confirm a corneal abrasion?

A. Fluorescein staining viewed under a blue light

B. Tonometry

C. Amsler grid

D. Gonioscopy

Answer: A. Fluorescein staining viewed under a blue light

Fluorescein dye stains areas where the corneal epithelium is missing, and under a cobalt blue light the abrasion glows green-yellow. This is the standard way to confirm corneal abrasion or ulcer in a welder with arc eye and pain after exposure. Tonometry measures eye pressure, the Amsler grid screens for macular problems, and gonioscopy examines the drainage angle. Teach to avoid rubbing the eye, to wear protective goggles at work, and to report worsening pain or vision. Do not use topical anesthetic drops at home.

B is wrong: Tonometry measures eye pressure.

C is wrong: The Amsler grid screens for macular problems.

D is wrong: Gonioscopy examines the drainage angle.

198. A client with retinal detachment is scheduled for scleral buckling. The nurse explains that this procedure involves:

A. Injecting a bubble of gas into the eye to block the hole

B. Applying a freezing probe to form a scar

C. Removing the cloudy lens and inserting an artificial lens

D. Sewing a silicone band onto the outside of the eye to push the eye wall against the detached retina

Answer: D. Sewing a silicone band onto the outside of the eye to push the eye wall against the detached retina

Scleral buckling treats retinal detachment by sewing a silicone band or sponge to the outside of the sclera, which indents the wall of the eye so that it meets the detached retina, often with cryopexy or laser to seal the break. Gas injection describes pneumatic retinopexy, freezing describes cryopexy, and lens removal describes cataract surgery. After the procedure the client may need to hold a head position, use drops, and avoid heavy lifting and bending. Report pain, nausea, or new floaters.

A is wrong: This describes pneumatic retinopexy.

B is wrong: This describes cryopexy.

C is wrong: This describes cataract extraction.

199. A client says he cleans deep inside his ears with cotton buds every day. The nurse advises:

A. Push the cotton bud deeper to get all the wax out

B. Use a hairpin instead of a cotton bud

C. Clean the ears with alcohol every day

D. Avoid putting cotton buds into the canal because they push wax deeper and can injure the ear

Answer: D. Avoid putting cotton buds into the canal because they push wax deeper and can injure the ear

Cotton buds, hairpins, and other objects pushed into the ear canal compress wax against the eardrum, causing impaction, and can scratch the canal or perforate the tympanic membrane. Alcohol every day dries the skin and can cause otitis externa. Ears are self-cleaning, so the nurse advises cleaning only the outer ear with a washcloth. Wax that blocks hearing can be softened with prescribed drops and removed by a professional. Memory aid: never put anything smaller than your elbow in your ear.

A is wrong: Deeper insertion raises the risk of impaction and perforation.

B is wrong: Hairpins can perforate the eardrum.

C is wrong: Daily alcohol dries and irritates the canal.

200. The nurse is irrigating an adult client's ear for impacted cerumen. Which technique is correct?

A. Use cold solution to reduce swelling

B. Aim the stream straight at the eardrum

C. Use solution at body temperature and aim the stream toward the upper wall of the ear canal

D. Seal the ear canal tightly with the syringe tip

Answer: C. Use solution at body temperature and aim the stream toward the upper wall of the ear canal

Warm irrigating solution at body temperature prevents the caloric effect that cold or hot fluid has on the inner ear, which would cause vertigo, nausea, and nystagmus. The stream is directed gently toward the upper wall of the canal, with the pinna pulled up and back in an adult, so that the fluid flows around the wax and pushes it out instead of striking the eardrum directly. Never occlude the canal with the syringe tip, since trapped pressure can rupture the tympanic membrane. Do not irrigate if a perforation is suspected. Instilling softening drops beforehand helps.

A is wrong: Cold solution causes vertigo and nausea.

B is wrong: A direct stream can rupture the eardrum.

D is wrong: Sealing the canal builds up pressure.

Nursing Research (200)

1. A nurse researcher studies "The effect of music therapy on postoperative pain among cesarean section mothers." What is the independent variable?

A. Postoperative pain

B. Music therapy

C. Cesarean section mothers

D. The hospital setting

Answer: B. Music therapy

The independent variable is the presumed cause or intervention, the one the researcher manipulates or studies to see its effect. Here music therapy is introduced to influence postoperative pain, so music therapy is independent and pain is the dependent variable, the outcome that is measured. Cesarean mothers are the population or subjects, and the hospital is the setting. Quick test: ask what is given or changed (independent) and what changes as a result (dependent). Memory aid: independent is the input, dependent depends on the input.

A is wrong: Pain is the outcome, the dependent variable.

C is wrong: The mothers are the population.

D is wrong: The setting is not a variable being tested.

2. Staff nurses improve their hand hygiene only during the weeks an infection-control researcher is visibly observing them. This is:

A. Hawthorne effect

B. Halo effect

C. Recall bias

D. Acquiescence bias

Answer: A. Hawthorne effect

The Hawthorne effect is a change in behavior simply because participants know they are being observed or studied, which threatens validity because the improved hand hygiene may not be their real habit. It is reduced by unobtrusive observation, longer observation periods and letting participants get used to the observer. The halo effect is rating a person on one good trait, recall bias is inaccurate memory of past events, and acquiescence bias is the tendency to agree with statements. Exam tip: the name comes from the Hawthorne factory studies, where output rose because workers were being watched.

B is wrong: The halo effect lets one good trait color the rating of others.

C is wrong: Recall bias is inaccurate memory of past events.

D is wrong: Acquiescence bias is a tendency to agree with statements.

3. A researcher divides 600 nurses by ward, then randomly selects nurses from each ward in proportion to its size. Which sampling technique is this?

A. Cluster sampling

B. Quota sampling

C. Stratified random sampling

D. Systematic sampling

Answer: C. Stratified random sampling

Stratified random sampling first divides the population into homogeneous strata, here wards, then randomly selects participants from each stratum, in proportion to its size if proportionate. This ensures every subgroup is represented and lowers sampling error. Cluster sampling randomly picks whole groups and studies all members, quota sampling is non-probability with fixed numbers per category chosen conveniently, and systematic sampling takes every kth person from a list. Tip: stratified means from each layer, cluster means whole groups. Stratified is a probability method, so findings can be generalized.

A is wrong: Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups, not individuals within each.

B is wrong: Quota sampling is non-random.

D is wrong: Systematic sampling picks every nth person from a list.

4. To study drug users who are hard to reach, a researcher asks each participant to refer others they know. This is:

A. Convenience sampling

B. Purposive sampling

C. Simple random sampling

D. Snowball sampling

Answer: D. Snowball sampling

Snowball (network) sampling is a non-probability technique in which current participants refer other people, so the sample grows like a rolling snowball. It is especially useful for hidden or hard-to-reach populations, such as drug users or persons with stigmatized conditions, where no sampling list exists. Its weakness is bias, because referred persons tend to resemble each other, so findings cannot be generalized. Convenience sampling uses whoever is available, purposive sampling selects people with specific traits chosen by the researcher, and simple random sampling needs a complete list. Tip: referrals mean snowball.

A is wrong: Convenience uses whoever is readily available.

B is wrong: Purposive picks people by the researcher's judgment of who fits.

C is wrong: Simple random needs a full list and equal chance for each.

5. A study explores "The lived experience of mothers caring for a child with leukemia." Which design fits best?

A. Ethnography

B. Phenomenology

C. Grounded theory

D. Quasi-experimental

Answer: B. Phenomenology

Phenomenology is a qualitative design that describes the meaning of lived experience from the participants' point of view, as with mothers caring for a child with leukemia. Data come from in-depth interviews, and the researcher uses bracketing to set aside personal assumptions. The guiding question is: what is it like? Ethnography studies a culture, grounded theory generates a theory about a social process, and quasi-experimental is a quantitative design that tests an intervention. Tip: lived experience means phenomenology, culture means ethnography, theory from data means grounded theory.

A is wrong: Ethnography studies a culture through immersion.

C is wrong: Grounded theory builds a theory about social processes.

D is wrong: Quasi-experimental is quantitative and tests interventions.

6. A researcher wants to develop a theory explaining how new nurses adapt to the night shift, based on their interviews. Which design is this?

A. Grounded theory

B. Phenomenology

C. Case study

D. Correlational

Answer: A. Grounded theory

Grounded theory is a qualitative design developed by Glaser and Strauss that builds a theory explaining a social process directly from the data, using interviews, constant comparison and coding until saturation. How new nurses adapt to the night shift is a process, so it can yield a theory. Phenomenology describes the meaning of an experience without building a theory, a case study examines one case or unit in depth, and correlational designs measure the relationship between variables statistically. Tip: the theory is grounded in the data, not set beforehand.

B is wrong: Phenomenology describes lived experience but does not build a theory.

C is wrong: A case study examines one person or unit in depth.

D is wrong: Correlational designs measure relationships between variables.

7. A study gives a new wound dressing to patients in Ward A and the usual dressing to Ward B. Patients are not randomly assigned. This design is:

A. True experimental

B. Pre-experimental

C. Quasi-experimental

D. Descriptive

Answer: C. Quasi-experimental

A quasi-experimental design tests an intervention with manipulation of the independent variable (the new dressing) but lacks random assignment and often a full control group, as when whole wards are used. A true experiment needs all three: manipulation, randomization and a control group. Pre-experimental designs, such as the one-shot case study, are weaker still, and descriptive studies only describe and do not test an intervention. Tip: count the features, and if manipulation exists but randomization is missing, it is quasi. Without random assignment, groups may differ at baseline, which weakens internal validity.

A is wrong: A true experiment needs randomization, manipulation and control.

B is wrong: Pre-experimental designs, like the one-shot case study, lack a comparison group.

D is wrong: Descriptive designs do not manipulate an intervention.

8. Which design isolates and controls the effect of taking a pretest?

A. One-shot case study

B. Pretest-posttest without control

C. Ex post facto

D. Solomon four-group design

Answer: D. Solomon four-group design

The Solomon four-group design combines the pretest-posttest control group design with a posttest-only control group design, so some groups take the pretest and others do not. Comparing them shows whether taking a pretest itself sensitized participants and influenced posttest scores (the testing effect). It is a true experimental design with randomization and is strong for internal and external validity, though it needs more participants. The one-shot case study and pretest-posttest without a control are pre-experimental and weak, and ex post facto looks back at existing differences without manipulation. Memory aid: Solomon means four groups.

A is wrong: The one-shot case study is the weakest design.

B is wrong: Without a control group, pretest effects cannot be separated.

C is wrong: Ex post facto is non-experimental and looks back from effect to cause.

9. A researcher selects patients with lung cancer and reviews their past records for smoking history. This design is:

A. Prospective

B. Retrospective (ex post facto)

C. Experimental

D. Longitudinal cohort

Answer: B. Retrospective (ex post facto)

A retrospective (ex post facto) design starts with the outcome, such as lung cancer, already present, and looks back at records or history to find possible causes such as smoking. Nothing is manipulated because the events have already happened. A prospective design starts with a possible cause or exposure and follows participants forward to see who develops the effect. Experimental designs manipulate an intervention, and a longitudinal cohort follows a group over time. In epidemiology this approach resembles the case-control study. Tip: effect first, then look back for the cause, means retrospective.

A is wrong: Prospective designs start with the cause and follow forward for the effect.

C is wrong: There is no manipulation, so it is not experimental.

D is wrong: A cohort follows people forward in time.

10. A study reports r = -0.85 between hours of sleep and stress scores. How should the nurse interpret this?

A. A strong negative relationship, but it does not prove that sleep causes lower stress

B. Lack of sleep causes stress

C. A weak relationship

D. No relationship

Answer: A. A strong negative relationship, but it does not prove that sleep causes lower stress

Pearson r ranges from negative 1.00 to positive 1.00. The sign shows direction and the size shows strength, so negative 0.85 is a strong inverse relationship: as hours of sleep go up, stress scores tend to go down. However, correlation shows association only, so it cannot prove that one variable causes the other, since a third variable or reverse direction may explain it. A value near zero means no linear relationship. Rule of thumb: 0.00 to 0.30 weak, 0.30 to 0.70 moderate, above 0.70 strong. Only experiments support cause and effect.

B is wrong: Correlation never proves causality.

C is wrong: 0.85 is strong, not weak.

D is wrong: Zero means no relationship, -0.85 is far from zero.

11. A blood pressure apparatus gives the same reading each time but is always 10 mmHg higher than the reference. The tool is:

A. Valid but not reliable

B. Neither reliable nor valid

C. Reliable but not valid

D. Both reliable and valid

Answer: C. Reliable but not valid

Reliability is consistency, the instrument gives the same result repeatedly, while validity is accuracy, whether it measures what it is supposed to measure. The apparatus gives the same readings each time, so it is reliable, but it is always 10 mmHg too high, so it systematically misses the true value and is not valid. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity: a tool must be reliable to be valid, yet a reliable tool can be consistently wrong. Memory aid: a scale that always reads 2 kg heavy is consistent but wrong. Hence nurses use calibrated equipment.

A is wrong: It is consistent, so it is reliable.

B is wrong: It is consistent, so it is reliable.

D is wrong: It is consistently wrong, so not valid.

12. Survey forms carry no names or codes, so even the researcher cannot link answers to respondents. This protects:

A. Confidentiality

B. Privacy

C. Informed consent

D. Anonymity

Answer: D. Anonymity

Anonymity means no one, including the researcher, can link the data to a participant because no names, codes or identifying details are recorded, which makes it the strongest protection of identity in research ethics. Confidentiality means the researcher knows who gave the information but promises not to reveal it, privacy is the right to control access to one's personal information, and informed consent is the voluntary agreement given after being told about the study. Tip: if even the researcher cannot tell who answered, it is anonymity. Anonymity is hard to achieve in interviews.

A is wrong: Confidentiality means the researcher knows identities but does not disclose them.

B is wrong: Privacy is the right to control access to oneself.

C is wrong: Consent is a separate right.

13. A study will include 9-year-old children. What is needed for ethical participation?

A. Consent of the child only

B. Parental consent plus the child's assent

C. Teacher's consent

D. Consent of the barangay captain

Answer: B. Parental consent plus the child's assent

A 9-year-old is a minor who cannot give legal consent, so the parents or legal guardian must give permission, and the child is also asked for assent, an affirmative agreement to take part that suits his or her level of understanding. Assent is usually sought from about age 7 years. If the child clearly declines, the researcher should respect this. This follows the ethical principle of respect for persons and the extra protection owed to vulnerable groups, including children, pregnant women, prisoners and persons with mental disability. Teachers, barangay officials or the child alone cannot give valid permission.

A is wrong: A minor cannot give legal consent alone.

C is wrong: Teachers cannot consent for children.

D is wrong: Local officials cannot consent for children.

14. A pain scale from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain) produces which level of measurement?

A. Nominal

B. Ratio

C. Ordinal

D. Interval

Answer: C. Ordinal

The levels of measurement are nominal (categories), ordinal (ranks), interval (equal intervals, no true zero) and ratio (equal intervals, true zero). A 0 to 10 pain scale ranks pain from low to high, but the gap between a 4 and a 5 may not match the gap between an 8 and a 9 in the client's experience, so the intervals are unequal and board exams classify it as ordinal. Likert scales, cancer stages and educational level are also ordinal. Memory aid: NOIR, nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio, from simplest to most precise.

A is wrong: Nominal data are categories with no order.

B is wrong: Ratio needs equal intervals and a true zero.

D is wrong: Interval needs truly equal spacing.

15. Which variable is measured at the ratio level?

A. Blood type

B. Educational attainment

C. Temperature in Celsius

D. Body weight in kilograms

Answer: D. Body weight in kilograms

Ratio level data have equal intervals and a true, absolute zero meaning none of the attribute, so ratios are meaningful: 80 kg is twice 40 kg. Weight, height, pulse rate, blood pressure and length of stay are ratio variables, as is temperature in Kelvin. Celsius is interval because zero degrees does not mean no heat, blood type is nominal because it only names categories, and educational attainment is ordinal because it ranks levels. Ratio data allow the widest range of statistical tests. Tip: if zero means none, it is ratio.

A is wrong: Blood type is nominal.

B is wrong: Educational attainment is ordinal.

C is wrong: Celsius has no true zero, so it is interval.

16. Monthly incomes of respondents are heavily skewed by a few very high earners. Which measure of central tendency best represents the data?

A. Mean

B. Median

C. Mode

D. Range

Answer: B. Median

The median is the middle value when scores are arranged in order, so it is not affected by extreme values. In skewed distributions such as income, a few very high earners pull the mean upward and give a misleading picture, so the median better represents the typical respondent. The mean is best for symmetrical interval or ratio data, the mode is the most frequent value and suits nominal data, and the range is a measure of variability, not central tendency. Tip: in a positively skewed distribution the mean is greater than the median, which is greater than the mode.

A is wrong: The mean is pulled by extreme values.

C is wrong: The mode is the most frequent value and may not represent the center.

D is wrong: Range measures spread, not central tendency.

17. A study with alpha set at 0.05 finds p = 0.03. What should the researcher conclude?

A. Reject the null hypothesis, the result is statistically significant

B. Accept the null hypothesis

C. The result is not significant

D. The study must be repeated

Answer: A. Reject the null hypothesis, the result is statistically significant

The decision rule is that if p is less than or equal to alpha, the null hypothesis is rejected. Alpha of 0.05 is the level of significance, the accepted risk of a Type I error. Since p of 0.03 is lower than 0.05, the result is statistically significant, meaning the finding is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so the null is rejected and the research hypothesis is supported. Statistical significance is not the same as clinical importance. Researchers never prove the null, they only reject it or fail to reject it. Tip: p low, null must go.

B is wrong: p is below alpha, so the null is rejected.

C is wrong: 0.03 is below 0.05, so it is significant.

D is wrong: Significance does not by itself call for repetition.

18. A researcher concludes a new drug works when, in reality, it does not. This is:

A. Type II error

B. Sampling error

C. Type I error

D. Measurement error

Answer: C. Type I error

A Type I error (alpha) is rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false positive: the researcher claims the drug works when it really does not. A Type II error (beta) is failing to reject a false null, a false negative, which means missing a real effect. Sampling error is natural variation between sample and population, and measurement error is inaccuracy of the tool. The chance of a Type I error is set in advance by alpha, usually 0.05. Memory aid: Type I is a false alarm, Type II is a miss. A larger sample size reduces Type II error.

A is wrong: A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject a false null.

B is wrong: Sampling error is the difference between sample and population values.

D is wrong: Measurement error concerns the instrument, not the decision.

19. A researcher wants to know if smoking status (smoker or non-smoker) is associated with sex (male or female). Which test is appropriate?

A. Independent t-test

B. Pearson r

C. ANOVA

D. Chi-square

Answer: D. Chi-square

Chi-square is the non-parametric test for comparing frequencies of two categorical (nominal) variables, such as smoking status and sex, to see whether they are associated. The independent t-test compares the means of two groups on a continuous variable, Pearson r measures the linear relationship of two interval or ratio variables, and ANOVA compares the means of three or more groups. Quick guide: nominal by nominal means chi-square, two means means t-test, three or more means means ANOVA, two continuous variables means correlation. Chi-square uses counts, not percentages.

A is wrong: The t-test compares means of interval or ratio data.

B is wrong: Pearson r needs interval or ratio data.

C is wrong: ANOVA compares means of 3 or more groups.

20. Which document first set voluntary consent as an absolute requirement for human research?

A. Declaration of Helsinki

B. Nuremberg Code

C. Belmont Report

D. Philippine Nursing Act

Answer: B. Nuremberg Code

The Nuremberg Code (1947) was created after the Nazi doctors' trials exposed cruel experiments on prisoners, and its first principle says the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. It laid the foundation of research ethics. The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) came later and guides physicians in research, while the Belmont Report (1979, United States) set out the three principles of respect for persons, beneficence and justice. The Philippine Nursing Act (RA 9173) governs practice, not research ethics. Tip: Nuremberg first, Helsinki next, Belmont third.

A is wrong: Helsinki came later and expanded guidance for medical research.

C is wrong: The Belmont Report came later in the United States.

D is wrong: RA 9173 regulates nursing practice, not research consent.

21. A reviewer at a Manila review center uses the VPADS framework to organize Nursing Research topics. In this framework, what does the letter A stand for?

A. Accuracy of research findings

B. Approach, whether quantitative or qualitative

C. Analysis of data using inferential tests

D. Assent of minors in research

Answer: B. Approach, whether quantitative or qualitative

VPADS is a review-center organizer for Nursing Research: Variables, Population and sampling, Approach, Designs, Scales and statistics. The A stands for Approach, meaning whether the study is quantitative (numbers, hypotheses, statistics) or qualitative (words, meaning, objectives). Knowing the approach first tells you which designs, sampling methods and tests are even possible. Exam tip: VPADS handles the technical building blocks of a study, while BRAVES handles quality and ethics, so sort every topic into one of the two mnemonics.

A is wrong: Accuracy belongs to the BRAVES framework, not VPADS.

C is wrong: Data analysis is not a separate letter of VPADS; statistics fall under S.

D is wrong: Assent is an ethics topic under BRAVES, not a VPADS letter.

22. A clinical instructor reviews the BRAVES framework with her students. Which topic belongs to VPADS rather than BRAVES?

A. Biases in research

B. Ethics in research

C. Variables

D. Validity versus reliability

Answer: C. Variables

BRAVES stands for Biases, Research process, Accuracy, Validity versus reliability, Ethics and Statistics, and it groups the quality, process and ethics topics of research. Variables, however, is the V of VPADS, which collects the technical building blocks of a study: Variables, Population and sampling, Approach, Designs and Scales. Variables are the characteristics measured or manipulated, such as independent, dependent and extraneous variables. Memory aid: if a topic is about what the study is built from, think VPADS, and if it is about how trustworthy or ethical the study is, think BRAVES.

A is wrong: Biases is the B of BRAVES.

B is wrong: Ethics is the E of BRAVES.

D is wrong: Validity versus reliability is the V of BRAVES.

23. ICU nurses at a tertiary hospital in Quezon City notice frequent ventilator-associated pneumonia and conduct a study to test whether a new oral care protocol reduces its incidence in their unit. This study is best classified as:

A. Tertiary research

B. Basic research

C. Historical research

D. Applied research

Answer: D. Applied research

Applied research is done to solve a practical, immediate problem, and here the ICU nurses test an oral care protocol to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia in their own unit. Basic (pure) research instead builds theory and knowledge without an immediate use. Nursing studies that test interventions, protocols or teaching programs are almost always applied. Exam tip: look for words such as solve, improve, reduce or test a protocol for applied research, and words such as explain, understand or build theory for basic research.

A is wrong: Tertiary refers to a type of data source, not a type of research.

B is wrong: Basic research extends the knowledge base of a discipline without an immediate practical goal.

C is wrong: Historical research establishes facts about past events.

24. A student nurse is writing a paper on the history of nursing in the Philippines. Which of the following is a PRIMARY source?

A. A nursing history textbook chapter

B. An encyclopedia entry on Philippine nursing

C. A transcript of her own interview with a retired nursing dean who practiced in the 1960s

D. A bibliography of articles on Philippine nursing

Answer: C. A transcript of her own interview with a retired nursing dean who practiced in the 1960s

A primary source is first-hand, original evidence created by the person who experienced or recorded the event, such as diaries, letters, photographs, official records and interview transcripts. The student's own interview with a retired dean who practiced in the 1960s gives raw testimony that no one has interpreted yet. Secondary sources analyze or interpret primary material, while tertiary sources compile or index other sources. Memory aid: primary equals raw and original, secondary equals interpreted, tertiary equals compiled for quick reference.

A is wrong: Textbooks describe and interpret information, so they are secondary sources.

B is wrong: Encyclopedias are compilations used for quick reference, so they are tertiary sources.

D is wrong: Bibliographies are compilations of sources, so they are tertiary.

25. A staff nurse searching for evidence on pressure injury prevention uses CINAHL and PubMed to locate articles. According to the handout, these databases are classified as:

A. Tertiary sources

B. Primary sources

C. Secondary sources

D. Raw field data

Answer: A. Tertiary sources

Tertiary sources are compilations, indexes or summaries of primary and secondary sources, and databases such as CINAHL and PubMed, along with encyclopedias, bibliographies and directories, belong here. They help the nurse locate and screen articles but are not the original research reports themselves. For evidence-based practice, use them to find studies, then read the primary reports and appraise their quality. Memory aid: primary is the original, secondary is the commentary, tertiary is the finding aid.

B is wrong: Primary sources are raw first-hand evidence, not indexes of articles.

C is wrong: Secondary sources describe or analyze primary sources, such as textbooks and literature reviews.

D is wrong: Raw field data is information gathered directly by the researcher.

26. A nurse at a government hospital in Caloocan has identified a high rate of 30-day readmissions among heart failure clients as her research problem. Following the research process in the handout, what is her NEXT step?

A. Collect data using a questionnaire

B. Review related literature

C. Disseminate the findings

D. Analyze the data

Answer: B. Review related literature

The research process follows a logical order: identify the problem, review related literature, formulate hypotheses or objectives, choose the design, collect data, analyze, interpret and disseminate. Once her problem of high heart failure readmissions is identified, the next step is the literature review to see what is already known, what has been tried and how others studied it. Doing this refines the problem and prevents duplicating prior work. Exam tip: when asked for the next step, find the step just after the one already completed in the sequence.

A is wrong: Data collection comes much later, after design and tool selection.

C is wrong: Dissemination is the final step.

D is wrong: Data cannot be analyzed before it is collected.

27. A nurse researcher asks herself whether she has enough time, funds, available subjects and institutional cooperation to finish her study before the end of the school year. Which criterion for evaluating a research problem is she considering?

A. Significance of the problem

B. Researchability of the problem

C. Interest to the researcher

D. Feasibility

Answer: D. Feasibility

Feasibility asks whether a study can realistically be completed with the time, money, subjects, facilities and cooperation available. The nurse's worry about funds, available respondents and the school-year deadline is exactly that practical question. The other criteria for a good research problem are significance (does it matter to nursing), researchability (can it be answered with empirical data), and the researcher's interest. Memory aid: feasibility equals can I actually finish this with what I have.

A is wrong: Significance asks whether the problem is important to nursing.

B is wrong: Researchability asks whether the problem can be studied using empirical data.

C is wrong: Interest refers to the personal curiosity and motivation of the researcher.

28. A nurse plans a phenomenological study on the lived experience of children left behind by OFW parents. What should guide this qualitative study?

A. A directional hypothesis

B. A null hypothesis tested at alpha 0.05

C. Broad, descriptive research objectives

D. A non-directional hypothesis

Answer: C. Broad, descriptive research objectives

Qualitative studies, including phenomenology, are guided by broad, descriptive research objectives or questions that explore meaning, while hypotheses that predict relationships are used in quantitative research. A phenomenological study of children left behind by OFW parents seeks lived experience, not to test a prediction or p value. Qualitative researchers stay open to what emerges from participants rather than fixing statistical expectations in advance. Exam tip: hypothesis goes with numbers and statistics, objectives go with words and meaning.

A is wrong: Hypotheses are used in quantitative research.

B is wrong: Null hypotheses are tested statistically in quantitative research.

D is wrong: Any type of hypothesis is used in quantitative, not qualitative, studies.

29. A nurse states: "Clients who receive structured discharge teaching will have fewer readmissions within 30 days than clients who receive routine teaching." This statement is a:

A. Directional hypothesis

B. Non-directional hypothesis

C. Null hypothesis

D. Research objective

Answer: A. Directional hypothesis

A directional hypothesis states the expected direction of the effect, such as one group having fewer, more, higher or lower outcomes. The statement predicts that structured discharge teaching leads to fewer readmissions than routine teaching, which names the better group. Hypotheses must state a relationship between variables and be testable. Memory aid: words like greater, less, fewer, higher or lower signal directional, while the words difference or relationship without a direction signal non-directional, and the words no difference signal null.

B is wrong: A non-directional hypothesis predicts a difference without stating which group will be higher or lower.

C is wrong: A null hypothesis predicts no relationship or difference.

D is wrong: An objective is a broad descriptive goal, not a testable prediction.

30. A researcher writes: "There will be a difference in medication adherence between hypertensive clients who receive SMS reminders and those who do not." This is classified as a:

A. Non-directional hypothesis

B. Directional hypothesis

C. Null hypothesis

D. Research problem

Answer: A. Non-directional hypothesis

A non-directional hypothesis predicts that a difference or relationship exists but does not say which group will be higher or lower. The statement says there will be a difference in adherence between the SMS and no-SMS groups without naming which is better, so it is non-directional. It is tested with two-tailed tests. Exam tip: if the words better, higher, lower, more or less are missing, and the statement is not worded as no difference, it is non-directional.

B is wrong: It would be directional only if it stated which group would have higher adherence.

C is wrong: A null hypothesis predicts no difference.

D is wrong: A research problem identifies a gap or issue needing investigation, not a predicted relationship.

31. A nurse studies whether breastfeeding education affects exclusive breastfeeding rates among mothers in a rural health unit in Bulacan. Which is the correctly stated NULL hypothesis?

A. Mothers who receive breastfeeding education will have higher exclusive breastfeeding rates.

B. There is a difference in exclusive breastfeeding rates between educated and non-educated mothers.

C. Breastfeeding education causes mothers to breastfeed longer.

D. There is no significant relationship between breastfeeding education and exclusive breastfeeding rates.

Answer: D. There is no significant relationship between breastfeeding education and exclusive breastfeeding rates.

The null hypothesis states that there is no significant relationship or difference between the variables, and it is the statement that statistical tests actually try to reject. The correct option says there is no significant relationship between breastfeeding education and exclusive breastfeeding rates. If the p value is less than alpha, the null is rejected and the alternative is supported. Memory aid: null means nothing, no difference and no effect, and it is always the starting assumption of inferential testing.

A is wrong: This is a directional alternative hypothesis.

B is wrong: This is a non-directional alternative hypothesis.

C is wrong: This is a causal claim, not a null prediction.

32. A study is titled "Effect of Early Ambulation on the Return of Bowel Function Among Post-Cesarean Mothers." What is the DEPENDENT variable?

A. Early ambulation

B. Post-cesarean mothers

C. Return of bowel function

D. The hospital where the study was done

Answer: C. Return of bowel function

The dependent variable is the outcome or effect that is measured and expected to change because of the independent variable. In this title, early ambulation is the intervention (independent variable), and return of bowel function is the result that depends on it. Mothers are the population and the hospital is the setting. Memory aid: ask what is being measured as the result, that is the dependent variable, and ask what is being given, changed or compared, that is the independent variable.

A is wrong: Early ambulation is the independent or treatment variable.

B is wrong: Post-cesarean mothers are the population, not a variable.

D is wrong: The setting is not a variable being measured.

33. A nurse researcher collects the age, sex, civil status, religion and years of service of staff nurses to describe the sample. These are called:

A. Demographic or attribute variables

B. Dependent variables

C. Extraneous variables

D. Confounding variables

Answer: A. Demographic or attribute variables

Demographic or attribute variables are preexisting characteristics of subjects, such as age, sex, civil status, religion and years of service, collected to describe the sample. They are usually reported as frequencies and percentages in the profile of respondents. They can also act as extraneous variables if they influence the outcome, but here their purpose is description. Exam tip: if the question lists personal characteristics collected to describe the respondents, the answer is demographic or attribute variables.

B is wrong: Dependent variables are the outcomes the researcher wants to explain.

C is wrong: Extraneous variables are factors that interfere with the results.

D is wrong: Confounding variables are uncontrolled extraneous variables.

34. In a study testing a health teaching program on glucose control, several participants also started a new herbal supplement on their own, which the researcher did not control. This uncontrolled factor is BEST called a:

A. Independent variable

B. Dependent variable

C. Demographic variable

D. Confounding variable

Answer: D. Confounding variable

A confounding variable is an extraneous variable that was not controlled and that influences the dependent variable, so the true effect of the intervention becomes unclear. The herbal supplements taken by participants can change glucose levels independently of the teaching program. Researchers control such variables through randomization, matching, restriction or statistical adjustment. Memory aid: confounders confuse the results, because they mix their effect with the independent variable.

A is wrong: The independent variable is the health teaching program.

B is wrong: The dependent variable is glucose control.

C is wrong: Demographic variables only describe the sample.

35. In a study of fatigue among emergency room nurses, which is the OPERATIONAL definition of fatigue?

A. A state of extreme tiredness resulting from mental or physical exertion

B. A feeling of weariness commonly experienced by health workers

C. A condition caused by long working hours

D. The total score on the 22-item Piper Fatigue Scale answered at the end of a 12-hour shift

Answer: D. The total score on the 22-item Piper Fatigue Scale answered at the end of a 12-hour shift

An operational definition tells exactly how a variable will be measured or observed in the study, naming the tool, scoring and conditions so another researcher can replicate it. Using a 22-item Piper Fatigue Scale total score after a 12-hour shift turns the abstract idea of fatigue into a measurable value. A conceptual definition, by contrast, is the dictionary or theoretical meaning. Exam tip: if the definition names an instrument, score, cut-off or procedure, it is operational.

A is wrong: This is a conceptual or dictionary-type definition.

B is wrong: This is a general description, not a measurement method.

C is wrong: This describes a possible cause, not how fatigue is measured.

36. A nurse wants to study adults with type 2 diabetes in Metro Manila but can only reach diabetic clients registered at three health centers in Caloocan. The registered clients at these three centers are the:

A. Target population

B. Sample

C. Accessible population

D. Sample size

Answer: C. Accessible population

The accessible population is the portion of the target population that the researcher can realistically reach, such as the diabetic clients registered at three Caloocan health centers. The target population is the whole group of interest, here all adults with type 2 diabetes in Metro Manila. The sample is then drawn from the accessible population. Findings generalize most safely to the accessible population, and less so to the target population. Memory aid: target is what you wish to study, accessible is what you can actually reach.

A is wrong: The target population is the entire group the researcher wants to generalize to.

B is wrong: The sample is the specific group actually selected from the accessible population.

D is wrong: Sample size is the number of participants, not a group.

37. A researcher obtains the official master list of 420 registered barangay health workers in a city, from which participants will be chosen. This list is called the:

A. Sampling frame

B. Sample size

C. Target population

D. Quota

Answer: A. Sampling frame

The sampling frame is the actual list of all members of the accessible population from which the sample is drawn, such as an official master list of 420 registered barangay health workers. A complete and accurate frame is needed for probability sampling like simple random, systematic and stratified sampling. Sample size is how many are chosen, and the target population is the group of interest, not the document itself. Memory aid: frame equals the list you pick from.

B is wrong: Sample size is the number of participants included in the study.

C is wrong: The target population is the whole group of interest, not the list itself.

D is wrong: A quota is a predetermined number per subgroup in quota sampling.

38. A nurse researcher selects every 5th client from the OPD admission log until 80 clients are chosen. This technique is:

A. Simple random sampling

B. Stratified sampling

C. Convenience sampling

D. Systematic sampling

Answer: D. Systematic sampling

Systematic sampling selects every kth member from an ordered list after a random start, here every 5th client in the OPD log. The sampling interval is computed as population size divided by sample size. It is a probability method that is simple and convenient, but hidden patterns in the list can bias results. Exam tip: the phrase every nth is the classic clue for systematic sampling.

A is wrong: Simple random sampling uses random numbers for every selection.

B is wrong: Stratified sampling first divides the population into subgroups.

C is wrong: Convenience sampling takes whoever is most accessible.

39. A researcher randomly selects 8 of the 188 barangays in Caloocan City and then surveys all households in the selected barangays. This is an example of:

A. Stratified sampling

B. Quota sampling

C. Cluster sampling

D. Systematic sampling

Answer: C. Cluster sampling

Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups (clusters), such as barangays, and then includes all or many members of those groups, which is efficient for large geographic areas. Stratified sampling, by contrast, divides the population by a characteristic and samples from every stratum. Here 8 of 188 barangays are randomly selected and all their households are surveyed, so entire units were chosen. Memory aid: cluster means pick whole clusters, stratified means pick some from every layer.

A is wrong: Stratified sampling selects individuals from every subgroup, not entire subgroups.

B is wrong: Quota sampling is non-random selection until a quota is filled.

D is wrong: Systematic sampling selects at regular intervals from a list.

40. A researcher wants 40 male and 60 female respondents and interviews any available OPD client until each number is reached. Which technique is being used?

A. Quota sampling

B. Stratified sampling

C. Purposive sampling

D. Snowball sampling

Answer: A. Quota sampling

Quota sampling is a non-probability technique in which the researcher sets the number of participants needed from each subgroup, such as 40 males and 60 females, and recruits whoever is available until each quota is filled. It resembles stratified sampling because it uses subgroups, but selection inside each subgroup is not random. Because it is non-random, it carries selection bias. Exam tip: subgroups plus convenience selection until the numbers are met equals quota sampling.

B is wrong: Stratified sampling uses random or systematic selection within each stratum.

C is wrong: Purposive sampling chooses participants most useful to the research purpose.

D is wrong: Snowball sampling recruits participants through other participants.

41. For a qualitative study, a researcher hand-picks staff nurses who have at least 5 years of experience in a COVID-19 ICU because they can give the most useful information. This technique is:

A. Purposive sampling

B. Convenience sampling

C. Cluster sampling

D. Systematic sampling

Answer: A. Purposive sampling

Purposive or judgmental sampling deliberately selects participants who can provide the richest information on the topic, based on stated inclusion criteria, such as ICU nurses with at least 5 years of COVID-19 experience. It is common in qualitative research, where depth of information matters more than generalizability. Non-probability methods include convenience, quota, purposive and snowball sampling. Memory aid: purposive equals chosen on purpose for what they know.

B is wrong: Convenience sampling takes whoever is most accessible, regardless of usefulness.

C is wrong: Cluster sampling is a probability technique selecting whole subgroups.

D is wrong: Systematic sampling selects at regular intervals from a list.

42. A researcher surveys nursing students who happen to be in the school lobby during lunch break. What is the MAIN disadvantage of this sampling technique?

A. It is expensive and time-consuming.

B. It requires a complete sampling frame.

C. It depends on participants recruiting other participants.

D. Results are not generalizable and are prone to selection and sampling bias.

Answer: D. Results are not generalizable and are prone to selection and sampling bias.

Convenience sampling takes whoever is easily available, such as students in the lobby, so the sample may not represent the population. Its main weakness is selection and sampling bias, which limits generalizability of the results even though it is quick and cheap. Probability sampling is preferred when results must be generalized. Exam tip: when the question asks for the main disadvantage of convenience sampling, answer that it is prone to bias and not generalizable.

A is wrong: Convenience sampling is actually easy and inexpensive.

B is wrong: Simple random sampling, not convenience sampling, requires a complete frame.

C is wrong: This describes snowball sampling.

43. Both stratified sampling and quota sampling divide the population into subgroups. What distinguishes STRATIFIED sampling?

A. Random or systematic selection is used within each subgroup.

B. Participants are recruited through referrals.

C. Entire subgroups are selected at random.

D. Participants are chosen by the researcher's judgment.

Answer: A. Random or systematic selection is used within each subgroup.

The key feature of stratified sampling is that after dividing the population into strata (such as year level, sex or unit), participants are chosen randomly or systematically within each stratum. This ensures every subgroup is represented in proportion and is a probability technique. Quota sampling also uses subgroups but fills them through non-random recruitment. Memory aid: stratified is random within layers, quota is convenience within layers.

B is wrong: This describes snowball sampling.

C is wrong: This describes cluster sampling.

D is wrong: This describes purposive sampling.

44. Which feature describes QUALITATIVE research based on the "Tell STORIES" mnemonic?

A. Structured tools such as tests and surveys

B. Coded numbers analyzed with statistics

C. Objective measurements presented in graphs

D. Textual data from interviews and focus group discussions analyzed interpretatively

Answer: D. Textual data from interviews and focus group discussions analyzed interpretatively

Qualitative research is described by the Tell STORIES mnemonic: it is subjective, uses textual data from interviews, observations and focus group discussions, and is analyzed interpretatively to explore meaning and experience. Quantitative research follows the Count SCORES features, namely structured tools, coded numbers, objective measures and statistics. Qualitative samples are usually small and purposive. Exam tip: words, themes and meaning point to qualitative, while numbers, tests and graphs point to quantitative.

A is wrong: Structured tools belong to Count SCORES, the quantitative mnemonic.

B is wrong: Coded numbers and statistics are quantitative features.

C is wrong: Objective measurements are quantitative features.

45. A nurse lives with an Aeta community in Zambales for six months to understand how their beliefs and rituals shape their healing practices. Which design is this?

A. Ethnography

B. Phenomenology

C. Grounded theory

D. Historical research

Answer: A. Ethnography

Ethnography studies the culture of a group through prolonged immersion and fieldwork, looking at beliefs, rituals, traditions and shared practices. A nurse living six months with an Aeta community to understand their healing beliefs fits this exactly. Phenomenology studies lived experience, and grounded theory builds a theory from data about a social process. Memory aid: ethno means people or culture, so ethnography equals describing a culture from the inside.

B is wrong: Phenomenology focuses on lived experience of a phenomenon, not culture.

C is wrong: Grounded theory develops a theory about social processes.

D is wrong: Historical research studies past events.

46. A study titled "The Evolution of Philippine Nursing Laws from 1919 to 2002" uses old laws, archives and records. Which design is this?

A. Ethnography

B. Case study

C. Phenomenology

D. Historical research

Answer: D. Historical research

Historical research systematically collects and evaluates records, documents, archives and artifacts to establish facts about past events. A study tracing Philippine nursing laws from 1919 to 2002 depends on old laws and archival records, not on living participants. Sources are judged by external criticism (is it authentic) and internal criticism (is it credible). Exam tip: past events, archives, documents and old records point to historical research.

A is wrong: Ethnography describes a living culture through immersion.

B is wrong: A case study is an in-depth analysis of a person, group or institution.

C is wrong: Phenomenology explores lived experience.

47. A head nurse in a medical ward and her staff introduce a new bedside endorsement protocol, then systematically study its effects in order to improve their own practice. This design is:

A. Case study

B. Action research

C. Grounded theory

D. Ethnography

Answer: B. Action research

Action research is practitioner-led and cyclical: identify a practice problem, introduce an action or change, study the effects and use findings to improve practice. The head nurse and her staff introducing a new endorsement protocol and evaluating it fit this pattern. It aims at local, immediate improvement rather than broad generalization. Memory aid: action research equals act, observe, reflect, then improve, and the participants are also the researchers.

A is wrong: A case study analyzes a single case in depth without introducing improvement cycles.

C is wrong: Grounded theory generates a theory about social processes.

D is wrong: Ethnography describes culture.

48. A nurse conducts an in-depth analysis of a single 12-year-old client with a rare genetic disorder and how his family copes with his care. This design is a:

A. Phenomenological study

B. Ethnographic study

C. Case study

D. Cross-sectional survey

Answer: C. Case study

A case study is an in-depth analysis of a single person, family, group or institution, often combining several data sources. A 12-year-old with a rare genetic disorder and the family coping with his care is one bounded case studied deeply. It gives rich detail but limited generalizability. Exam tip: the words single case or in-depth analysis of one unit point to a case study, while many subjects at one time point means a cross-sectional survey.

A is wrong: Phenomenology explores lived experience across several participants.

B is wrong: Ethnography describes a culture.

D is wrong: A cross-sectional survey collects data from many subjects at one point in time.

49. In a study on burnout among nurses, the researcher combines in-depth interviews, direct observation and a standardized burnout questionnaire in a single investigation. This approach is called:

A. Triangulation

B. Solomon four-group design

C. Snowball sampling

D. Concealment

Answer: A. Triangulation

Triangulation combines multiple data sources, methods, investigators or theories in one study to strengthen the credibility of findings and offset the weaknesses of any single approach. Using in-depth interviews, observation and a standardized questionnaire on burnout is methodological triangulation. When different methods lead to similar conclusions, confidence in the findings increases. Memory aid: tri means three viewpoints on the same question.

B is wrong: The Solomon four-group design is a true experimental design with four groups.

C is wrong: Snowball sampling is a recruitment technique.

D is wrong: Concealment is collecting data without participants' knowledge.

50. Which set of characteristics is required for a TRUE experimental design?

A. Manipulation, observation and survey

B. Randomization, manipulation and a control group

C. Random sampling, interviews and observation

D. Manipulation only, without a comparison group

Answer: B. Randomization, manipulation and a control group

A true experiment needs three elements: manipulation of the independent variable, randomization (random assignment to groups) and a control or comparison group. These features give the strongest evidence of cause and effect because they control selection bias and extraneous variables. Designs lacking randomization are quasi-experimental, and those lacking a control group or randomization are pre-experimental. Memory aid: MRC, manipulation, randomization and control.

A is wrong: Observation and survey are data collection methods, not design requirements.

C is wrong: Interviews and observation describe data collection, not experimental features.

D is wrong: Without randomization and a control group, the design is quasi or pre-experimental.

51. A single group of barangay health workers attends a dengue prevention seminar and then answers a knowledge test afterward. There is no pretest and no comparison group. This design is a:

A. One-shot case study, a pre-experimental design

B. Posttest-only control group design

C. Solomon four-group design

D. Quasi-experimental design with comparison group

Answer: A. One-shot case study, a pre-experimental design

The one-shot case study applies a treatment to a single group and then measures the outcome once, with no pretest and no comparison group. It is a pre-experimental design and the weakest because there is nothing to compare the posttest against, so improvement cannot be attributed to the seminar. History, maturation and selection threaten it. Exam tip: one group, treatment, then posttest only equals one-shot case study.

B is wrong: A posttest-only control group design requires random assignment and a control group.

C is wrong: The Solomon design uses four randomly assigned groups.

D is wrong: There is no comparison group in this study.

52. A nurse surveys pregnant women at a rural health unit during March 2026 to determine the prevalence of anemia at that point in time. This is a:

A. Longitudinal survey

B. Prospective cohort study

C. Retrospective study

D. Cross-sectional survey

Answer: D. Cross-sectional survey

A cross-sectional survey collects data from subjects at a single point in time, which makes it suited for describing prevalence. Surveying pregnant women in March 2026 to determine the prevalence of anemia at that moment is the classic use. It is quick and inexpensive, but it cannot show how a condition changes over time or prove cause and effect. Memory aid: cross-sectional is a snapshot, longitudinal is a movie.

A is wrong: Longitudinal surveys follow subjects over an extended period.

B is wrong: Prospective studies follow subjects forward into the future.

C is wrong: Retrospective studies look back at past causes.

53. A researcher assesses the motor and cognitive development of preterm infants every 6 months for 5 years using repeated measures. This design is:

A. Cross-sectional

B. Longitudinal

C. Ex post facto

D. One-shot case study

Answer: B. Longitudinal

A longitudinal study collects data from the same subjects repeatedly over an extended period, which allows the researcher to describe change and development. Assessing preterm infants every 6 months for 5 years is repeated measures over time. It is useful for growth and development but costly and prone to attrition (dropout). Exam tip: the key terms follow-up, over time and repeated measures point to longitudinal designs.

A is wrong: Cross-sectional studies collect data at a single point in time.

C is wrong: Ex post facto studies look back to the past for causes.

D is wrong: A one-shot case study is a pre-experimental design.

54. A researcher identifies nurses currently working permanent night shifts and nurses working day shifts, then follows both groups for 3 years to see who develops hypertension. This design is:

A. Retrospective

B. Cross-sectional

C. Prospective

D. Historical

Answer: C. Prospective

A prospective study identifies the presumed cause or exposure in the present and follows subjects forward in time to see whether the effect develops. Following night-shift and day-shift nurses for 3 years to see who develops hypertension moves from exposure to outcome. This resembles a cohort study and gives stronger evidence of temporality than retrospective designs. Memory aid: prospective looks ahead, retrospective looks back.

A is wrong: Retrospective studies identify the effect first and look back for the cause.

B is wrong: Cross-sectional studies collect data at one point in time.

D is wrong: Historical research studies past events, not health outcomes over time.

55. In a retrospective or ex post facto study, what does the researcher identify FIRST?

A. The dependent variable or effect in the present, then searches the past for its cause

B. The cause in the present, then follows subjects into the future

C. An intervention that is randomly assigned to subjects

D. The variables to be manipulated

Answer: A. The dependent variable or effect in the present, then searches the past for its cause
