In a retrospective or ex post facto study, the effect or outcome is already present, so the researcher identifies the dependent variable first and then looks backward to find possible causes, often through chart review or interviews. The researcher cannot manipulate anything, since the events have already occurred. This makes it vulnerable to recall bias and confounding. Memory aid: retro means backward, so start with the outcome and trace back the cause.

B is wrong: This describes a prospective study.

C is wrong: Random assignment of interventions is a feature of experiments.

D is wrong: There is no manipulation in non-experimental designs.

56. A study finds a correlation coefficient of 0.62 between hours of nurse overtime and number of medication errors. The researcher concludes that overtime causes medication errors. What is the BEST critique?

A. The coefficient is too weak to be meaningful.

B. A positive coefficient means the variables move in opposite directions.

C. Chi-square should have been used instead.

D. The result shows a moderate positive association, but correlation does not prove causation.

Answer: D. The result shows a moderate positive association, but correlation does not prove causation.

A correlation coefficient of 0.62 shows a moderate positive relationship, meaning the two variables tend to increase together, but correlation never proves causation. Without manipulation, randomization or control of extraneous factors, other variables such as staffing, fatigue or workload could explain medication errors. The coefficient ranges from minus 1 to plus 1, and its sign gives direction while its size gives strength. Exam tip: reject any answer that claims a correlation proves that one variable causes another.

A is wrong: A coefficient of 0.62 indicates a moderate relationship, not a negligible one.

B is wrong: A positive coefficient means both variables increase together.

C is wrong: Chi-square is for nominal data, while these variables are ratio.

57. Which statement BEST describes the VALIDITY of a research instrument?

A. It gives consistent results on repeated use.

B. It produces stable scores over time.

C. Two raters obtain the same scores.

D. It actually reflects the construct or variable being examined.

Answer: D. It actually reflects the construct or variable being examined.

Validity is the degree to which an instrument measures what it is supposed to measure, meaning it truly reflects the construct under study. Types include content, criterion-related and construct validity. A tool can be reliable without being valid, but it cannot be valid unless it is reliable. Memory aid: validity equals accuracy, reliability equals consistency.

A is wrong: Consistency describes reliability.

B is wrong: Stability over time is test-retest reliability.

C is wrong: Agreement between raters is interrater reliability.

58. A researcher gives an anxiety questionnaire to the same group of nursing students twice, two weeks apart, and correlates the two sets of scores. What is being tested?

A. Content validity

B. Interrater reliability

C. Test-retest reliability

D. Construct validity

Answer: C. Test-retest reliability

Test-retest reliability measures the stability of an instrument by giving the same tool to the same subjects at two different times and correlating the scores. Giving the anxiety questionnaire twice, two weeks apart, fits this procedure. A high correlation shows stable results over time. The interval should be long enough to prevent memory effects, yet short enough that the trait has not truly changed. Memory aid: test, wait, retest.

A is wrong: Content validity is judged by experts reviewing items.

B is wrong: Interrater reliability compares two observers rating the same thing.

D is wrong: Construct validity tests whether the tool measures a theoretical concept.

59. A researcher asks a panel of maternal and child nursing experts to review whether the items of a breastfeeding knowledge questionnaire adequately cover all aspects of the topic. This establishes:

A. Test-retest reliability

B. Content validity

C. Interrater reliability

D. Internal consistency

Answer: B. Content validity

Content validity is the extent to which the items of an instrument adequately cover all aspects of the concept being measured. It is usually established by a panel of experts who review the items, as with the maternal and child nursing experts here, often with a content validity index. It is a form of validity, not reliability, because it asks whether the right content is included. Exam tip: experts reviewing item coverage equals content validity.

A is wrong: Test-retest reliability involves repeated administration over time.

C is wrong: Interrater reliability compares observers, not item coverage.

D is wrong: Internal consistency is computed statistically, such as with Cronbach alpha.

60. A researcher asks: "Was the new discharge program really the cause of fewer readmissions, or were there other factors?" This question is about:

A. External validity

B. Reliability

C. Internal validity

D. Content validity

Answer: C. Internal validity

Internal validity asks whether the independent variable really caused the observed change in the dependent variable, or whether other factors such as history, maturation, selection or testing explain it. The question about whether the discharge program was truly the cause is exactly this concern. Strong designs with randomization, control groups and standardized procedures protect it. Memory aid: internal validity is about cause inside the study, external validity is about generalizing outside it.

A is wrong: External validity concerns generalizability to other populations and settings.

B is wrong: Reliability concerns consistency of measurement.

D is wrong: Content validity concerns the coverage of instrument items.

61. A nurse wants to apply findings from a study done in a private tertiary hospital in Makati to clients in rural health units in Samar. Her concern is MAINLY with:

A. Internal validity

B. Test-retest reliability

C. Interrater reliability

D. External validity

Answer: D. External validity

External validity is the extent to which study findings can be generalized to other populations, settings and times. Applying results from a private tertiary hospital in Makati to rural health units in Samar raises a question of whether the results will hold in a very different setting. Representative sampling and replication in various settings strengthen it. Exam tip: the words generalize, apply to other settings or different population point to external validity.

A is wrong: Internal validity concerns whether the IV caused the outcome.

B is wrong: Test-retest reliability concerns stability of an instrument.

C is wrong: Interrater reliability concerns agreement between raters.

62. During a 3-month study on a school-based handwashing program, the DOH launches a nationwide handwashing campaign on television. This is a threat to internal validity called:

A. Maturation

B. Testing

C. History

D. Instrumentation

Answer: C. History

History is a threat to internal validity in which an external event occurring during the study influences the outcome, so the effect cannot be credited to the intervention alone. The DOH nationwide television campaign during the school handwashing study is such an event. A randomized control group helps because both groups experience the same event. Memory aid: history equals something happened in the world during the study.

A is wrong: Maturation refers to natural changes within subjects over time.

B is wrong: Testing refers to the effect of taking a pretest on later scores.

D is wrong: Instrumentation refers to changes in the measuring tool or observers.

63. A Filipino nurse researcher conducting a drug trial is guided by a globally recognized document that sets ethical standards for medical research involving human subjects and was adopted by the World Medical Association. This document is the:

A. Nuremberg Code

B. Belmont Report

C. Declaration of Helsinki

D. Code of Ethics for Filipino Nurses

Answer: C. Declaration of Helsinki

The Declaration of Helsinki, adopted by the World Medical Association, is the international statement of ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects, including identifiable human material and data. It stresses informed consent, risk-benefit assessment, protection of vulnerable groups and review by an ethics committee. It builds on the Nuremberg Code, which came from the Nazi doctors trial. In the Philippines, it works alongside national research ethics guidelines and the Data Privacy Act. Exam tip: Helsinki equals WMA and medical research.

A is wrong: The Nuremberg Code arose from war crimes trials and emphasizes voluntary consent.

B is wrong: The Belmont Report is a United States report that outlines respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

D is wrong: The Code of Ethics for Filipino Nurses governs nursing practice, not international medical research.

64. A researcher enrolls only charity ward clients in a high-risk drug trial because they are easier to recruit, while paying clients are excluded. Which ethical principle is MOST violated?

A. Justice

B. Beneficence

C. Respect for persons

D. Veracity

Answer: A. Justice

Justice requires fair selection of participants and fair distribution of research burdens and benefits. Enrolling only charity ward clients because they are easier to recruit places the risks of a high-risk trial on a vulnerable, convenient group while excluding others who could benefit or share the risk. Subjects should be chosen for scientific reasons, not for ease or vulnerability. Memory aid: justice equals fairness in selection and treatment.

B is wrong: Beneficence concerns maximizing benefits and minimizing harm, but the main issue is unfair selection.

C is wrong: Respect for persons concerns autonomy and consent.

D is wrong: Veracity concerns truth-telling.

65. During an interview on grief, a participant becomes very distressed. The nurse researcher stops the interview and refers her to a counselor. Which principle is the nurse upholding?

A. Justice

B. Anonymity

C. Beneficence and the right to freedom from harm

D. Full disclosure

Answer: C. Beneficence and the right to freedom from harm

Beneficence is the duty to do good and prevent harm, and it includes the right to protection from discomfort and harm, whether physical, emotional, social or financial. Stopping the interview when the participant became distressed and referring her to a counselor puts her welfare above the data. Researchers must weigh risks against benefits and minimize risks. Exam tip: the nurse acting to prevent or reduce harm to the participant equals beneficence.

A is wrong: Justice concerns fair selection and treatment.

B is wrong: Anonymity concerns not linking identity to data.

D is wrong: Full disclosure concerns explaining the study before consent.

66. Halfway through a study, a participant tells the nurse researcher she no longer wants to continue. What is the BEST response?

A. Ask her to finish because her data are needed for the sample size.

B. Respect her decision and allow her to withdraw without any penalty.

C. Tell her that withdrawal will affect her hospital care.

D. Offer her a larger cash incentive to stay.

Answer: B. Respect her decision and allow her to withdraw without any penalty.

The right to self-determination means participation must be voluntary, and a participant may decline, ask questions, refuse to answer and withdraw at any time without penalty. The best response is to respect her decision and assure her that her care will not be affected. Any pressure, threat or inducement undermines voluntariness. Researchers must honor withdrawal even if it reduces the sample size. Memory aid: the participant is free to join and free to leave.

A is wrong: Pressuring her violates self-determination.

C is wrong: Threatening her care is coercion.

D is wrong: Excessive rewards to stay are also a form of coercion.

67. A researcher offers indigent clients 20,000 pesos each to join a high-risk drug trial. The ethics board objects mainly because this:

A. Constitutes coercion through excessive reward

B. Violates anonymity

C. Is a form of concealment

D. Is a Type I error

Answer: A. Constitutes coercion through excessive reward

Coercion is an overt or implied threat or an excessive reward that compromises free choice. A payment of 20,000 pesos offered to indigent clients for a high-risk drug trial is an undue inducement, because poverty may push them to accept risks they would otherwise refuse. Ethics boards review compensation so that it reimburses time and effort without overriding judgment. Memory aid: too good to refuse, especially for the poor, equals coercion.

B is wrong: Payment does not involve linking identity to data.

C is wrong: Concealment is collecting data without participants' knowledge.

D is wrong: Type I error is a statistical concept.

68. According to the handout, informed consent is based on which TWO rights?

A. Right to privacy and right to anonymity

B. Right to self-determination and right to full disclosure

C. Right to confidentiality and right to compensation

D. Right to justice and right to freedom from harm

Answer: B. Right to self-determination and right to full disclosure

Informed consent rests on two rights: the right to self-determination (voluntary decision) and the right to full disclosure (being told the nature, purpose, risks, benefits and procedures of the study). Its elements include information, comprehension, competence and voluntariness. Consent must be documented, usually in writing, and obtained before any data collection. Memory aid: consent equals freedom to choose plus complete information to choose with.

A is wrong: Privacy and anonymity protect data, not the basis of consent.

C is wrong: Compensation is not a basis of informed consent.

D is wrong: These are important rights but not the stated basis of consent.

69. An elderly client who speaks only Ilocano signs an English consent form after the researcher reads it quickly in English. Which element of informed consent is MOST lacking?

A. Comprehension of the information

B. Voluntariness

C. Competence

D. Full disclosure of benefits

Answer: A. Comprehension of the information

Valid informed consent requires that participants understand the information given, which means it must be presented in a language and manner they can follow. An Ilocano-speaking elderly client who only hears a rapid English reading cannot truly comprehend the study, so her signature is not meaningful consent. The researcher should use the Ilocano language, simple wording and a translator if needed, and should confirm understanding by asking questions. Exam tip: a signed form alone does not equal informed consent.

B is wrong: Nothing suggests she was forced.

C is wrong: An elderly adult is presumed competent unless shown otherwise.

D is wrong: The information was presented, but not in a way she understood.

70. A researcher observes the behavior of relatives in a hospital waiting area through a one-way window without their knowledge, because she fears they would act differently if they knew. This practice is called:

A. Deception

B. Concealment

C. Anonymity

D. Debriefing

Answer: B. Concealment

Concealment is the collection of data without the participants' knowledge that they are being studied, so no consent is obtained. Watching relatives through a one-way window without their knowledge is concealment, and it raises concerns about privacy and consent. It can be acceptable only in limited circumstances, such as minimal risk and approval by an ethics board. Memory aid: concealment hides the fact of the study itself, while deception hides or falsifies details about it.

A is wrong: Deception is deliberately giving false information about the study.

C is wrong: Anonymity means identity cannot be linked to data.

D is wrong: Debriefing is explaining the study after participation.

71. A researcher tells participants that a study is about general dietary habits, when it is actually about symptoms of eating disorders. This practice is BEST described as:

A. Concealment

B. Confidentiality

C. Deception

D. Full disclosure

Answer: C. Deception

Deception means deliberately withholding information or giving false information about the purpose or nature of a study. Telling participants the study concerns general dietary habits when it actually examines eating disorder symptoms misleads them about the real purpose, although they know they are being studied. It is allowed only when justified, with minimal risk, ethics approval and debriefing afterward. Memory aid: deception equals lying about the details, concealment equals secretly watching.

A is wrong: Concealment involves collecting data without participants knowing they are being studied at all.

B is wrong: Confidentiality is a pledge not to disclose identifying information.

D is wrong: Full disclosure is the opposite of misinforming participants.

72. A nurse researcher knows the identity of each interviewee but assigns codes in the report and keeps the master list locked so that no one else can identify participants. Which protection is being applied?

A. Anonymity

B. Concealment

C. Assent

D. Confidentiality

Answer: D. Confidentiality

Confidentiality is a pledge that the participant's information will not be revealed in any way that identifies them, even though the researcher knows who they are. Using codes in the report and keeping the master list locked is the standard practice. Anonymity requires that even the researcher cannot link data to participants, as in unsigned mailed questionnaires. Exam tip: if the researcher knows the identity, it cannot be anonymity, so choose confidentiality.

A is wrong: Anonymity exists only when even the researcher cannot link participants to data.

B is wrong: Concealment is collecting data without participants' knowledge.

C is wrong: Assent is a child's agreement to participate.

73. A researcher interviews adolescent mothers in a private room of the health center and asks only questions needed for the study objectives. Which right is MAINLY protected?

A. Right to privacy

B. Right to full disclosure

C. Right to compensation

D. Right to anonymity

Answer: A. Right to privacy

The right to privacy means participants' personal information and behavior are not intruded upon more than necessary, and that study questions and settings respect their dignity. Interviewing adolescent mothers in a private room and asking only items needed for the objectives limits intrusion. The Data Privacy Act of 2012 supports this principle in health research. Privacy concerns how much is asked and where, while confidentiality concerns how the data are protected afterward.

B is wrong: Full disclosure concerns explaining the study before consent.

C is wrong: Compensation is not the issue here.

D is wrong: The researcher still knows who the mothers are, so this is not anonymity.

74. Parents of an 11-year-old consent to his participation in a non-therapeutic study, but the child clearly says he does not want to join. What should the nurse researcher do?

A. Enroll him because parental consent is legally sufficient.

B. Respect the child's refusal and do not enroll him.

C. Offer him a toy so he will agree.

D. Enroll him but exclude his data later.

Answer: B. Respect the child's refusal and do not enroll him.

Assent is a child's affirmative agreement to take part in research, and it is sought in addition to parental permission from about age 7. If an 11-year-old clearly refuses in a non-therapeutic study, which offers him no direct benefit, he must not be enrolled even with parental consent. Offering rewards to change his mind would amount to coercion. Under Philippine law, the legal age of majority is 18, so parents or guardians give permission, but the child's dissent is still respected. Memory aid: parents consent, the child assents.

A is wrong: Parental consent alone ignores the need for the child's assent.

C is wrong: Giving a reward to change his mind is coercive.

D is wrong: Enrolling him disregards his refusal.

75. A nurse supervisor gives a staff nurse excellent ratings in all areas of her performance appraisal, including clinical skills, because the nurse is always punctual and pleasant. This is an example of:

A. Horn effect

B. Central tendency bias

C. Halo effect

D. Acquiescence bias

Answer: C. Halo effect

The halo effect is a rater bias in which one positive trait, such as punctuality and pleasantness, causes the rater to score the person high in unrelated areas like clinical skills. Performance appraisals should evaluate each criterion separately and use objective evidence. Training raters and using behavioral rating scales reduce it. Memory aid: halo is an angelic glow that makes everything look good, while the horn effect is the devil's horns that make everything look bad.

A is wrong: The horn effect involves a single negative trait influencing overall judgment.

B is wrong: Central tendency places most ratings in the middle.

D is wrong: Acquiescence is a respondent's tendency to agree.

76. A clinical instructor rates a student poorly in all areas of clinical performance because the student once submitted a care plan late. This is an example of:

A. Halo effect

B. Horn effect

C. Recall bias

D. Pygmalion effect

Answer: B. Horn effect

The horn effect, also called the reverse halo effect, occurs when one negative trait, such as submitting a single late care plan, unfairly lowers the rater's evaluation of all other areas. It is the opposite of the halo effect. Clinical instructors and supervisors reduce it by rating each competency on its own evidence and over a period of time. Memory aid: horns equal one bad thing darkens everything.

A is wrong: The halo effect is driven by a positive trait.

C is wrong: Recall bias involves inaccurate memory of past events.

D is wrong: The Pygmalion effect involves expectations influencing performance.

77. On a survey of health center services, many respondents agree with almost every statement, especially items they are unsure about. This is:

A. Acquiescence bias

B. Central tendency bias

C. Courtesy bias

D. Selection bias

Answer: A. Acquiescence bias

Acquiescence bias, also called agreement bias or yea-saying, is the tendency of respondents to agree with statements regardless of content, especially when unsure. It inflates agreement on surveys and may be reduced by mixing positively and negatively worded items and by using clear questions. Courtesy bias is different, because it involves politeness toward the questioner. Memory aid: acquiescence equals always saying yes.

B is wrong: Central tendency bias places responses in the middle of a scale.

C is wrong: Courtesy bias is not stating unhappiness in order to be polite.

D is wrong: Selection bias arises from non-random selection of the sample.

78. Clients in a charity ward tell the nurse interviewer that they are satisfied with the care, even though they had complaints, because they do not want to seem ungrateful to her. This is:

A. Social desirability bias

B. Recall bias

C. Courtesy bias

D. Dunning-Kruger effect

Answer: C. Courtesy bias

Courtesy bias occurs when respondents hide their dissatisfaction to be polite or avoid offending the interviewer, as when charity ward clients avoid seeming ungrateful to the nurse. It is common in satisfaction surveys and in cultures that value politeness and gratitude, including the Filipino hiya and utang na loob values. Using anonymous self-administered forms or interviewers who are not providers can reduce it. Exam tip: the keywords polite, grateful or not wanting to offend point to courtesy bias.

A is wrong: Social desirability concerns answering to be viewed favorably by others, not politeness to the questioner about a service.

B is wrong: Recall bias involves inaccurate memory.

D is wrong: Dunning-Kruger is overestimation of one's own ability.

79. A head nurse rating staff on a 5-point scale marks almost every item as 3, the middle of the scale. This error is called:

A. Halo effect

B. Central tendency bias

C. Acquiescence bias

D. Horn effect

Answer: B. Central tendency bias

Central tendency bias is a rater's habit of avoiding extreme scores and placing most ratings in the middle of the scale. A head nurse marking almost every item as 3 on a 5-point scale fails to discriminate between strong and weak performers. Even-numbered scales with no neutral midpoint and rater training can reduce it. Memory aid: central tendency equals playing it safe in the middle.

A is wrong: The halo effect raises all ratings because of one positive trait.

C is wrong: Acquiescence is agreeing with statements when in doubt.

D is wrong: The horn effect lowers all ratings because of one negative trait.

80. In a survey on risky behaviors, senior high school students under-report smoking and alcohol use so that they will be seen in a good light. This is:

A. Courtesy bias

B. Recall bias

C. Selection bias

D. Social desirability bias

Answer: D. Social desirability bias

Social desirability bias is the tendency of respondents to answer in ways that make them look good to others, so socially unacceptable behaviors like smoking and drinking are under-reported. Students giving cleaner answers than the truth in a risky behavior survey is typical. Anonymous questionnaires, assurance of confidentiality and indirect questioning reduce it. Exam tip: the keywords seen in a good light or looking good point to social desirability.

A is wrong: Courtesy bias concerns politeness toward a questioner about a service.

B is wrong: Recall bias concerns inaccurate memory of past events.

C is wrong: Selection bias concerns how the sample was chosen.

81. A researcher strongly expects the intervention group of nursing students to perform better, and unconsciously gives them more encouragement during testing. Their scores improve. This is the:

A. Hawthorne effect

B. Rosenthal or Pygmalion effect

C. Halo effect

D. Dunning-Kruger effect

Answer: B. Rosenthal or Pygmalion effect

The Rosenthal or Pygmalion effect is the influence of the researcher's expectations on participants' performance or on the measured outcome, as when unconscious extra encouragement leads the intervention group to score better. Blinding of researchers and data collectors and standardized scripts reduce this bias. The Hawthorne effect, by contrast, arises from participants knowing they are observed. Memory aid: Pygmalion equals high expectations produce high results.

A is wrong: The Hawthorne effect is behavior change due to awareness of being observed.

C is wrong: The halo effect is a rater bias from one positive trait.

D is wrong: Dunning-Kruger is overestimation of one's own ability.

82. Mothers of children with leukemia are asked to remember what household chemicals they were exposed to during pregnancy, about 6 years ago. Which bias is MOST likely?

A. Recall bias

B. Hawthorne effect

C. Central tendency bias

D. Halo effect

Answer: A. Recall bias

Recall bias is a systematic error in which participants do not remember past events accurately or omit details, and it is common in retrospective studies. Mothers asked about chemical exposures during a pregnancy 6 years ago may forget or, having a sick child, recall more intensely than others. Using records, shorter recall periods and structured prompts help. Exam tip: asking about the distant past in case-control or retrospective designs points to recall bias.

B is wrong: The Hawthorne effect involves being observed.

C is wrong: Central tendency involves ratings in the middle of a scale.

D is wrong: The halo effect is a rater bias.

83. Newly hired nurses rate their own IV insertion skills as the highest in the unit, yet they obtain the lowest scores on the actual skills validation. This illustrates:

A. Halo effect

B. Courtesy bias

C. Pygmalion effect

D. Dunning-Kruger effect

Answer: D. Dunning-Kruger effect

The Dunning-Kruger effect is a cognitive bias in which people with low skill or experience overestimate their own competence because they lack the knowledge needed to recognize their errors. New nurses who rate their IV insertion highest but score lowest on validation illustrate this gap. Objective skills validation, feedback and preceptorship help correct it. Memory aid: the less you know, the more confident you may feel.

A is wrong: The halo effect concerns judging others based on one positive trait.

B is wrong: Courtesy bias concerns politeness to a questioner.

C is wrong: The Pygmalion effect concerns researcher expectations influencing outcomes.

84. In an experiment, the researcher worries that differences in results might be due to differences among subjects rather than the treatment. What is the BEST way to control this selection bias?

A. Increase the number of observers

B. Use random assignment of subjects to groups

C. Use a convenience sample

D. Give a pretest only to the experimental group

Answer: B. Use random assignment of subjects to groups

Selection bias occurs when subjects in compared groups differ from the start, so outcomes may reflect those differences rather than the treatment. Random assignment gives every subject an equal chance of being in either group, which distributes known and unknown characteristics evenly. Convenience sampling, more observers or pretesting one group do not achieve this. Exam tip: randomization is the best single control for selection bias and for extraneous variables.

A is wrong: More observers do not equalize the groups.

C is wrong: Convenience sampling increases selection bias.

D is wrong: Pretesting one group does not equalize the groups.

85. A study records the blood type of each blood donor at a Red Cross chapter. What is the level of measurement of blood type?

A. Ordinal

B. Interval

C. Ratio

D. Nominal

Answer: D. Nominal

Nominal data are classified into named categories with no order or numeric meaning, such as blood type, sex, religion and marital status. Blood types A, B, AB and O cannot be ranked or measured. Only counts, frequencies and mode can be computed, and chi-square is the usual test. Memory aid: the levels of measurement go NOIR, nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio, from the simplest to the most precise.

A is wrong: Ordinal data can be ranked, but blood types have no order.

B is wrong: Interval data have equal intervals, which blood type lacks.

C is wrong: Ratio data have a true zero, which does not apply.

86. A study measures body temperature in degrees Celsius of febrile children. Why is this classified as INTERVAL and not ratio data?

A. Temperature in Celsius cannot be ranked.

B. Zero degrees Celsius is not the absence of temperature, so there is no true zero.

C. The intervals between degrees are unequal.

D. Temperature can only be categorized.

Answer: B. Zero degrees Celsius is not the absence of temperature, so there is no true zero.

Interval data have equal spacing between values but no true zero, which means ratios are not meaningful. Zero degrees Celsius is simply a point on the scale and does not mean no heat, so 40 degrees is not twice as hot as 20. Kelvin has an absolute zero and is therefore ratio. Other interval examples are IQ scores and calendar years. Memory aid: interval has equal gaps but a false zero, ratio has a real zero.

A is wrong: Celsius values can be ranked.

C is wrong: The intervals between degrees are equal.

D is wrong: This describes nominal data.

87. A researcher records the monthly household income in pesos of families in a barangay. According to the handout, the level of measurement is:

A. Nominal

B. Ordinal

C. Ratio

D. Interval

Answer: C. Ratio

Ratio data have equal intervals and a true zero, meaning zero represents total absence of the quantity. Household income in pesos qualifies, because zero pesos means no income and 20,000 pesos is twice 10,000. Other ratio examples are age, weight, height, pulse rate and length of stay. Ratio data allow every statistical test, including mean, standard deviation and t-test. Exam tip: if you can say twice as much and zero means none, it is ratio.

A is wrong: Income has order and equal intervals, so it is more than nominal.

B is wrong: Income has equal intervals, not just ranks.

D is wrong: Income has a true zero, so it is ratio rather than interval.

88. A nurse records the number of prenatal visits of five mothers: 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. What is the MEAN?

A. 6

B. 8

C. 10

D. 40

Answer: B. 8

The mean is the arithmetic average, computed by adding all values and dividing by the number of values. Here 4 plus 6 plus 8 plus 10 plus 12 equals 40, and 40 divided by 5 equals 8. Because the values are evenly spaced, the mean equals the median. The mean is sensitive to extreme values, so for skewed data the median is preferred. Memory aid: mean is the fair share, add everything and divide by how many.

A is wrong: 6 is one of the values, not the average.

C is wrong: 10 is one of the values, not the average.

D is wrong: 40 is the sum, not the mean.

89. Two classes took the same pharmacology exam. Class A has a standard deviation of 3 and Class B has a standard deviation of 12. What can the researcher conclude?

A. Class A has more variable scores and a wider variance.

B. Class B has more variable scores and a wider variance.

C. Class B has a higher mean score.

D. Both classes have the same spread of scores.

Answer: B. Class B has more variable scores and a wider variance.

Standard deviation measures how far scores typically lie from the mean, so a larger SD means greater spread and variability. Class B, with an SD of 12, has more widely scattered scores than Class A with an SD of 3, whose scores cluster tightly around the mean. SD says nothing about whether the mean is high or low. Variance is the square of the SD. Memory aid: small SD means scores are homogeneous, large SD means scores are heterogeneous.

A is wrong: Class A has the smaller SD, so its scores are less spread out.

C is wrong: SD describes spread, not the level of the mean.

D is wrong: Different SDs mean different spreads.

90. A researcher compares the mean systolic blood pressure of 50 hypertensive clients taking amlodipine and 50 separate clients taking losartan. Which test is MOST appropriate?

A. Paired t-test

B. Chi-square

C. Independent t-test

D. Spearman rho

Answer: C. Independent t-test

The independent t-test compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups on an interval or ratio outcome, such as blood pressure in clients taking amlodipine versus clients taking losartan. The groups contain different people, so the samples are independent. The paired t-test applies only when the same subjects are measured twice or are matched. Exam tip: two different groups and means equals independent t-test.

A is wrong: The paired t-test is for the same group measured twice.

B is wrong: Chi-square is for nominal data.

D is wrong: Spearman rho tests correlation of ordinal or non-normal data.

91. Barangay health workers took a knowledge test before and after a training on hypertension screening. To compare their pretest and posttest mean scores, the researcher should use the:

A. Independent t-test

B. ANOVA

C. Chi-square

D. Dependent or paired t-test

Answer: D. Dependent or paired t-test

The dependent or paired t-test compares two means from the same group measured twice, as with pretest and posttest scores of the same barangay health workers. Because the scores are related, the test works on the differences within pairs. It assumes interval or ratio data that are roughly normal. Exam tip: before and after in the same people equals paired t-test, and three or more groups equals ANOVA.

A is wrong: The independent t-test compares two separate groups.

B is wrong: ANOVA compares three or more groups.

C is wrong: Chi-square is for nominal data.

92. A researcher compares the mean NCLEX-style mock exam scores of first-year, second-year, third-year and fourth-year nursing students. Which test is MOST appropriate?

A. ANOVA

B. Independent t-test

C. Paired t-test

D. Pearson r

Answer: A. ANOVA

ANOVA, analysis of variance, compares the means of three or more independent groups using one test, which avoids the inflated error that comes from running many t-tests. Four year levels of nursing students make four groups, so ANOVA is the best choice. A significant result tells you that at least one group differs, and post hoc tests such as Tukey show which. Memory aid: two groups use t-test, three or more groups use ANOVA.

B is wrong: The t-test compares only two groups.

C is wrong: The paired t-test is for the same group measured twice.

D is wrong: Pearson r tests a relationship, not a difference in means.

93. A researcher wants to determine the relationship between age and systolic blood pressure among 200 adults; both variables are normally distributed ratio data. Which test should be used?

A. Chi-square

B. Spearman rho

C. Pearson r

D. Paired t-test

Answer: C. Pearson r

Pearson r tests the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables, interval or ratio, that are approximately normally distributed. Age and systolic blood pressure of 200 adults meet those conditions. The coefficient ranges from minus 1 to plus 1. Chi-square handles nominal data, and Spearman rho is the substitute for ordinal or non-normal data. Exam tip: relationship plus normal ratio data equals Pearson r.

A is wrong: Chi-square is for nominal variables.

B is wrong: Spearman is for ordinal or non-normally distributed data.

D is wrong: The paired t-test compares means, not relationships.

94. A researcher examines the relationship between clients' ranked satisfaction level (low, moderate, high) and their ranked compliance level (poor, fair, good). Which test is MOST appropriate?

A. Pearson r

B. Spearman rho

C. Independent t-test

D. ANOVA

Answer: B. Spearman rho

Spearman rho is the non-parametric correlation test for ordinal data, or for interval or ratio data that are not normally distributed. Ranked satisfaction (low, moderate, high) and ranked compliance (poor, fair, good) are both ordinal, so Spearman fits. Pearson r requires continuous normal data. Like Pearson, Spearman ranges from minus 1 to plus 1. Memory aid: Spearman for ranks, Pearson for precise measurements.

A is wrong: Pearson r requires normally distributed interval or ratio data.

C is wrong: The t-test compares means of two groups.

D is wrong: ANOVA compares means of three or more groups.

95. Which of the following is a NON-PARAMETRIC test?

A. Independent t-test

B. ANOVA

C. Pearson r

D. Chi-square

Answer: D. Chi-square

Chi-square is a non-parametric test used for nominal or categorical data, comparing observed frequencies with expected frequencies. Parametric tests, namely the t-test, ANOVA and Pearson r, assume interval or ratio data and a roughly normal distribution. Other non-parametric options include Spearman rho, Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank. Exam tip: categories and counts mean chi-square, and means mean parametric.

A is wrong: The t-test is parametric.

B is wrong: ANOVA is parametric.

C is wrong: Pearson r is parametric.

96. A study on the effect of a stress management program yields a p value of 0.12, with the significance level set at 0.05. What is the CORRECT conclusion?

A. Reject the null hypothesis; the program is effective.

B. Fail to reject the null hypothesis; the result is not statistically significant.

C. Accept the alternative hypothesis.

D. A Type I error has been proven.

Answer: B. Fail to reject the null hypothesis; the result is not statistically significant.

The decision rule is to reject the null hypothesis only when the p value is less than or equal to the significance level (alpha). A p value of 0.12 is greater than 0.05, so the researcher fails to reject the null and the result is not statistically significant, meaning there is not enough evidence that the program works. Failing to reject does not prove the null true. Memory aid: if p is low, the null must go.

A is wrong: The p value is greater than alpha, so the null cannot be rejected.

C is wrong: The alternative is accepted only when the null is rejected.

D is wrong: A single p value does not prove that an error occurred.

97. A researcher sets the confidence level of her study at 99 percent. What is the corresponding significance level, alpha?

A. 1 percent or 0.01

B. 5 percent or 0.05

C. 10 percent or 0.10

D. 99 percent or 0.99

Answer: A. 1 percent or 0.01

The significance level (alpha) equals 1 minus the confidence level, so a 99 percent confidence level gives an alpha of 0.01, or 1 percent. Alpha is the probability of making a Type I error, which is rejecting a true null hypothesis. A smaller alpha makes the test stricter but raises the chance of a Type II error. Common pairs to memorize are 95 percent confidence with 0.05 alpha and 90 percent confidence with 0.10 alpha.

B is wrong: 5 percent corresponds to a 95 percent confidence level.

C is wrong: 10 percent corresponds to a 90 percent confidence level.

D is wrong: This is the confidence level, not alpha.

98. A new dengue vaccine truly reduces infection, but a small study concludes that it has no significant effect and fails to reject the null hypothesis. What error was committed?

A. Type I error, a false positive

B. Sampling frame error

C. Type II error, a false negative

D. Hawthorne effect

Answer: C. Type II error, a false negative

A Type II error (beta error, false negative) happens when a false null hypothesis is not rejected, so a real effect is missed. The vaccine truly works, but the small study concluded no significant effect, which is often caused by low statistical power from a small sample. Increasing sample size raises power. A Type I error is the opposite, a false positive, rejecting a true null. Memory aid: Type I means falsely finding an effect, Type II means missing a real one.

A is wrong: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis.

B is wrong: A sampling frame error concerns the list used to select subjects.

D is wrong: The Hawthorne effect concerns behavior change from being observed.

99. A nurse researcher presents a poster of her completed study at a national nursing convention and submits a manuscript to a nursing journal. This is which step of the research process?

A. Interpretation and conclusion

B. Data analysis

C. Review of related literature

D. Dissemination

Answer: D. Dissemination

Dissemination is the last step of the research process, in which results are shared with target audiences through journal articles, poster and oral presentations, conferences and application in practice. Presenting a poster at a national convention and submitting a manuscript to a journal accomplish this. Sharing findings allows other nurses to use evidence in practice and allows others to critique and replicate the study. Memory aid: research that is not shared cannot change practice.

A is wrong: Interpretation compares results with the hypothesis and explains meaning.

B is wrong: Data analysis presents results in tables, graphs or thematic maps.

C is wrong: The literature review happens at the start of the study.

100. A researcher wants to collect data on health practices from elderly residents in a barangay, many of whom cannot read. Which data collection method is MOST appropriate?

A. Self-administered questionnaire

B. Structured interview

C. Online survey

D. Mailed questionnaire

Answer: B. Structured interview

An interview, where the researcher asks questions orally and records the answers, is the most suitable method for respondents who cannot read or write, such as many elderly residents. It also lets the researcher clarify questions and observe nonverbal cues. Written forms, whether self-administered, online or mailed, assume literacy, and online or mailed surveys also need access and a good return rate. Exam tip: when literacy is limited, choose a face-to-face interview in the local language.

A is wrong: Self-administered questionnaires require the ability to read.

C is wrong: Online surveys require literacy and internet access.

D is wrong: Mailed questionnaires require literacy.

101. A nurse researcher in a Pasig tertiary hospital develops a scoring tool to identify which newly admitted elderly clients are most likely to develop pressure injuries within one week. Which purpose of research does this study MAINLY serve?

A. Prediction

B. Description

C. Explanation

D. Control

Answer: A. Prediction

Prediction means using known factors to forecast what will happen, and a scoring tool that identifies which clients will develop pressure injuries does exactly that. The four purposes of research are description, explanation, prediction and control. Description answers what exists, explanation answers why, prediction answers what will happen, and control answers how to make it happen or prevent it. Memory aid: D-E-P-C, from what, to why, to will, to how. Risk assessment tools such as the Braden Scale are classic examples of predictive research tools in nursing.

B is wrong: Description only portrays the phenomenon as it exists, it does not forecast who will develop it.

C is wrong: Explanation clarifies why a phenomenon happens rather than forecasting its occurrence.

D is wrong: Control involves manipulating conditions to change outcomes, which this tool does not do.

102. Biologists and nurse scientists in a university laboratory study how specific growth factors regulate collagen formation in healing tissue, with no immediate plan to change bedside practice. This study is BEST classified as:

A. Applied research

B. Basic research

C. Action research

D. Historical research

Answer: B. Basic research

Basic or pure research aims to extend the knowledge base of a discipline, such as how growth factors regulate collagen formation, without an immediate practical use. Applied research, in contrast, solves a specific practical problem and its findings are used right away in a real setting. Often basic findings later become the foundation of applied studies and evidence-based practice. Exam tip: look for the phrase no immediate application or advance theory, which signals basic research, and for solve a problem or improve practice, which signals applied research.

A is wrong: Applied research aims to solve a practical problem in a real setting, which is not the stated goal.

C is wrong: Action research is practitioner-led and aims to improve practice in a specific setting.

D is wrong: Historical research establishes facts about past events, not current biological mechanisms.

103. A nurse researcher in Iloilo repeats a published Cebu study on kangaroo mother care using the same methods and obtains similar results. This repetition MAINLY demonstrates which quality expected of research knowledge?

A. Replicability

B. Anonymity

C. Feasibility

D. Generalizability to all populations

Answer: A. Replicability

Replicability is the quality of research knowledge that allows other researchers to repeat the same methods and obtain similar results. Good research knowledge should be accurate, replicable, credible and trustworthy, so it can stand up to scrutiny. Replication is how a single finding becomes accepted evidence for practice, as in repeating a kangaroo mother care study in another city. Note that a single repetition does not prove that findings apply to every population, since generalizability needs representative sampling across many settings.

B is wrong: Anonymity is an ethical protection of participants, not a quality of findings.

C is wrong: Feasibility is a criterion for judging whether a research problem can be studied.

D is wrong: One repetition in one setting does not prove the findings apply to all populations.

104. A student nurse writing a paper on medication errors gathers several materials. Which one is a SECONDARY source?

A. Incident reports filed by staff nurses in her base hospital

B. Her own interview transcripts with nurses who committed medication errors

C. A journal article that reviews and analyzes several published studies on medication errors

D. Photographs of mislabeled medication cups taken during her observation

Answer: C. A journal article that reviews and analyzes several published studies on medication errors

A secondary source describes, interprets, evaluates or analyzes information that came from primary sources, so a review article that synthesizes several published studies is secondary. A primary source gives first-hand, original evidence such as raw data, official records, interview transcripts, photographs taken by the researcher, or the original research report. Memory aid: primary means straight from the source or the eyewitness, secondary means someone else's summary. Textbooks, encyclopedias, reviews and commentaries are common secondary sources.

A is wrong: Incident reports are official records that provide first-hand evidence, so they are primary.

B is wrong: Interview transcripts are raw, first-hand data and are primary sources.

D is wrong: Photographs taken during observation are first-hand evidence and are primary sources.

105. When writing the review of related literature for her thesis, a nurse researcher is advised to rely mainly on primary research reports rather than on textbooks. What is the BEST reason?

A. Primary reports give the original findings and methods without another author's interpretation

B. Textbooks are never accepted as references in nursing

C. Primary reports are always shorter and easier to read

D. Primary sources do not need to be cited in the reference list

Answer: A. Primary reports give the original findings and methods without another author's interpretation

Primary research reports present the original methods, data and findings, so the reviewer can judge their quality directly rather than depend on another author's interpretation, which may contain errors or bias. In a review of related literature, nursing researchers are advised to rely mainly on primary sources and to use secondary sources for background or to locate primary studies. Both kinds of sources may be cited, and every source used must appear in the reference list. Reading original studies also strengthens critical appraisal skills needed in evidence-based practice.

B is wrong: Textbooks can be cited for background, they are simply secondary sources.

C is wrong: Length and readability are not the reason for preferring primary sources.

D is wrong: All sources used must be cited, whether primary or secondary.

106. A researcher plans to study 75 percent of the 240 senior nursing students of a college in Manila. How many students make up the sample size?

A. 180

B. 160

C. 75

D. 200

Answer: A. 180

Sample size is the number of participants actually included in a study. To get it, convert the percentage to a decimal and multiply by the population: 0.75 times 240 equals 180. Always check that the answer is a count of persons and not the percentage itself. A quick check is that 75 percent should be three quarters of the total, and one quarter of 240 is 60, so three quarters is 180. Expect similar computation items in the board exam on sample size, sampling interval and proportional allocation.

B is wrong: 160 is about 67 percent of 240, not 75 percent.

C is wrong: 75 is the percentage, not the number of students.

D is wrong: 200 is about 83 percent of 240, not 75 percent.

107. A nurse researcher writes the names of all 90 staff nurses of a district hospital on slips of paper, places them in a box, and draws 30 names without looking. This technique is:

A. Systematic sampling

B. Convenience sampling

C. Quota sampling

D. Simple random sampling

Answer: D. Simple random sampling

Simple random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected, and drawing names from a box is the lottery or fishbowl method. It requires a complete list of the population, here the 90 staff nurses, and a truly random draw with no human choice involved. It is a probability sampling technique, which supports generalizing findings to the population. Memory aid: lottery, fishbowl, table of random numbers or computer generated numbers all point to simple random sampling.

A is wrong: Systematic sampling selects individuals at regular intervals from a numbered list.

B is wrong: Convenience sampling takes whoever is most accessible, not a random draw.

C is wrong: Quota sampling fills preset numbers per subgroup by non-random selection.

108. A researcher has a numbered list of 500 clients enrolled in a TB-DOTS program and needs a systematic sample of 50. What sampling interval should she use?

A. Every 5th client

B. Every 50th client

C. Every 10th client

D. Every 25th client

Answer: C. Every 10th client

In systematic sampling the sampling interval is computed as the population size divided by the desired sample size, so 500 divided by 50 gives every 10th client. The researcher then picks a random starting point within the first interval and selects every 10th name on the numbered list. This is a probability method that is easy to carry out when a complete ordered list exists. Check your answer by multiplying the interval by the sample size, which should return the population size, as 10 times 50 equals 500.

A is wrong: Every 5th client would yield 100 clients, twice the needed sample.

B is wrong: Every 50th client would yield only 10 clients.

D is wrong: Every 25th client would yield only 20 clients.

109. A hospital has 600 nurses: 150 in critical care, 300 in medical-surgical wards, and 150 in other units. Using proportional stratified sampling, the researcher selects a total sample of 120. How many critical care nurses should be included?

A. 30

B. 40

C. 60

D. 15

Answer: A. 30

In proportional stratified sampling, each stratum is represented in the sample in the same proportion as in the population. The sampling fraction is the sample size divided by the population size, 120 divided by 600 equals 0.20, and this is applied to each stratum. Critical care contributes 0.20 times 150, or 30 nurses, medical-surgical 60 and other units 30, totaling 120. Always add up the strata sample sizes to confirm they equal the total. Stratification improves representativeness when the population has distinct subgroups.

B is wrong: 40 would over-represent critical care nurses relative to their share of the population.

C is wrong: 60 is the correct number for the 300 medical-surgical nurses, not critical care.

D is wrong: 15 is only 10 percent of the critical care nurses.

110. In which situation is CLUSTER sampling MOST appropriate?

A. The researcher needs a list of every individual to draw names by lottery

B. The researcher wants participants who are experts on a rare condition

C. The researcher must reach a hidden population through referrals

D. The population is spread across many similar barangays and no complete list of individual residents exists

Answer: D. The population is spread across many similar barangays and no complete list of individual residents exists

Cluster sampling is used when the population is spread over a wide area and a complete list of individuals is unavailable, so the researcher randomly selects whole groups such as barangays, schools or wards and studies the members of those clusters. It saves time and cost in community-based studies. Compare it with the other methods: lists of individuals suit simple random sampling, experts suit purposive sampling, and referrals suit snowball sampling. Exam tip: geographic units such as barangays or districts strongly suggest cluster sampling.

A is wrong: Drawing names from a complete list of individuals describes simple random sampling.

B is wrong: Hand-picking experts describes purposive sampling.

C is wrong: Reaching hidden populations through referrals describes snowball sampling.

111. A nurse researcher states that she will hand-pick participants who can best answer her research question. According to the handout, what must be clearly stated for this sampling technique?

A. The sampling interval

B. The size of each cluster

C. The random number table used

D. Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Answer: D. Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Purposive or judgment sampling is a non-probability method in which the researcher deliberately chooses participants who can best provide the needed information. Because selection depends on the researcher's judgment, the inclusion and exclusion criteria must be clearly stated so that readers know who qualified and why. It is common in qualitative research where information-rich cases matter more than representativeness. Remember that findings from purposive samples cannot be statistically generalized to a population.

A is wrong: A sampling interval is used in systematic sampling.

B is wrong: Cluster size applies to cluster sampling.

C is wrong: Random number tables apply to probability sampling, not purposive sampling.

112. Which of the following is the BEST written research hypothesis?

A. Incentive spirometry is good for the lungs

B. Postoperative clients who perform incentive spirometry 10 times every hour will have fewer atelectasis cases than those who do not

C. Nurses should teach incentive spirometry to all clients

D. Is incentive spirometry useful after surgery?

Answer: B. Postoperative clients who perform incentive spirometry 10 times every hour will have fewer atelectasis cases than those who do not

A good hypothesis is clear, specific, testable and measurable, and it states the expected relationship between variables, preferably including the population, intervention and outcome. The correct item names the intervention (incentive spirometry done 10 times every hour), the comparison (those who do not), and the measurable outcome (fewer atelectasis cases). Vague value statements, recommendations and questions are not hypotheses. Memory aid: a hypothesis predicts, a research question asks, and a recommendation advises.

A is wrong: This statement is vague and does not specify measurable variables.

C is wrong: This is a recommendation or value statement, not a testable prediction.

D is wrong: This is a question, not a predictive statement.

113. A staff nurse in a pediatric ward notices that children whose mothers stay overnight seem to cry less during IV insertion, and she decides to study this. What is the source of her research problem?

A. Existing theory

B. Personal experience

C. Previous research

D. Literature sources

Answer: B. Personal experience

The source of her research problem is personal experience, since the idea came from her own observation in clinical practice. Sources of research problems include personal experience, the literature, existing theories and previous research. Nurses are well placed to find problems because they notice patterns at the bedside, such as children crying less when mothers stay overnight. Once the observation is noted, the next step would be to review the literature to see whether it has already been studied and then refine it into a researchable question.

A is wrong: She did not start from a theory.

C is wrong: She did not base the problem on a prior study.

D is wrong: She did not derive the problem from published literature.

114. A nurse proposes to study the question, "Should euthanasia be legalized in the Philippines?" Her adviser rejects it. Which criterion for evaluating a research problem is MOST lacking?

A. Interest to the researcher

B. Significance

C. Feasibility of the budget

D. Researchability

Answer: D. Researchability

A researchable problem can be answered by collecting and analyzing observable data. Questions about what should or ought to be done, such as whether euthanasia should be legalized, involve moral and value judgments that data cannot settle, although the related attitudes and practices of people could be studied. The other criteria are significance, feasibility (time, money, subjects, cooperation, facilities and the researcher's expertise), interest to the researcher, and ethical acceptability. Exam tip: words like should, ought and better in moral terms signal a non-researchable question.

A is wrong: The nurse is clearly interested in the topic.

B is wrong: The issue is socially significant.

C is wrong: The main issue is not cost but that the question cannot be answered with data.

115. A researcher chooses to study hypertension self-management because it affects a large proportion of Filipino adults and the findings could improve nursing practice and health policy. Which criterion for a research problem is being emphasized?

A. Researchability

B. Feasibility

C. Significance of the problem

D. Interest to the researcher

Answer: C. Significance of the problem

Significance of the problem refers to its importance, including the number of people affected and its potential contribution to nursing practice, education, administration and health policy. Hypertension affects a large proportion of Filipino adults, so the study has broad relevance. Feasibility asks whether the study can be carried out with the available time, funds, subjects and cooperation, while researchability asks whether data can answer the question. Memory aid: significance equals so what, meaning why it matters and to whom.

A is wrong: Researchability concerns whether data can answer the question.

B is wrong: Feasibility concerns time, funds, subjects and cooperation.

D is wrong: Personal interest concerns the researcher's own motivation.

116. While reviewing related literature, a nurse discovers that her exact study, with the same variables, setting and population, was completed two years ago. Which purpose of the literature review does this BEST illustrate?

A. Establishing the level of measurement of the variables

B. Computing the sample size

C. Finding out whether the research has already been duplicated

D. Obtaining informed consent from participants

Answer: C. Finding out whether the research has already been duplicated

One purpose of reviewing related literature is to find out whether a study has already been done, which prevents unnecessary duplication of effort and shows what is already known. The review also gives a foundation for the study, helps refine the research problem, identifies gaps, and guides the choice of theory, design and instruments. Discovering an identical study means the researcher should modify the problem, such as using a different population or setting. Sample size and consent belong to the methodology and data collection stages, not to the literature review.

A is wrong: Levels of measurement are determined by how variables are measured, not by the literature search.

B is wrong: Sample size computation is part of methodology.

D is wrong: Informed consent is obtained from participants during data collection.

117. A researcher bases her study of self-care among clients on hemodialysis on Dorothea Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory. This existing theory, used to guide the study, serves as the:

A. Conceptual definition

B. Theoretical framework

C. Operational definition

D. Sampling frame

Answer: B. Theoretical framework

A theoretical framework is based on an existing, established theory, such as Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory, which guides the study's questions, variables and interpretation. A conceptual framework, by contrast, is constructed by the researcher from related concepts when no single theory fits. Memory aid: theoretical means borrowed from a named theorist, conceptual means built by the researcher. In nursing research, theories from Orem, Roy, Neuman, Peplau and Watson are frequently used as theoretical frameworks.

A is wrong: A conceptual definition is the dictionary-type meaning of a single variable.

C is wrong: An operational definition states how one variable will be measured.

D is wrong: A sampling frame is a list of people from whom the sample is drawn.

118. In a Philippine undergraduate thesis, the researchers draw an input-process-output diagram showing how their own selected concepts and study variables relate to one another. This diagram is BEST called the:

A. Theoretical framework

B. Review of related literature

C. Data collection instrument

D. Conceptual framework or research paradigm

Answer: D. Conceptual framework or research paradigm

A conceptual framework, often presented as a research paradigm or input-process-output diagram, is the researcher's own structure of concepts and variables and how they relate in the study. It maps out the independent and dependent variables and guides data collection and analysis. A theoretical framework is instead anchored on a published theory. This is common in Philippine undergraduate theses, where the IPO model is used to show the flow from inputs such as variables, through the process of the study, to the expected output.

A is wrong: A theoretical framework is based on an established theory rather than the researcher's own arrangement of concepts.

B is wrong: The review of related literature is the narrative summary of previous works.

C is wrong: An instrument is the tool used to gather data.

119. Which is a CONCEPTUAL definition of pain?

A. The score from 0 to 10 on a numeric pain rating scale taken 2 hours after surgery

B. An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage

C. The number of times the client requested analgesics in 24 hours

D. The client's facial expression score using the FLACC scale

Answer: B. An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage

A conceptual definition gives the dictionary or theoretical meaning of an abstract concept, such as pain being an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. An operational definition states how the concept will be measured in the study, such as a score on a numeric rating scale or the FLACC tool. Memory aid: conceptual tells what it means, operational tells how it is measured. Both definitions should appear in a research proposal so that variables are clear and measurable.

A is wrong: A numeric rating scale score is an operational definition.

C is wrong: Counting analgesic requests is an operational definition.

D is wrong: A FLACC score is an operational definition.

120. In a study on the effect of a walking program on blood glucose, the researcher includes only clients who are not taking insulin, because insulin use could also affect blood glucose. Insulin use in this study is a/an:

A. Independent variable

B. Dependent variable

C. Extraneous variable that the researcher is controlling

D. Demographic variable used only to describe the sample

Answer: C. Extraneous variable that the researcher is controlling

An extraneous variable is one other than the independent and dependent variables that could affect the results. Restricting the sample to clients who do not use insulin controls this variable by eliminating its influence. If it were not controlled, it could become a confounding variable that muddles the effect of the walking program. Other ways to control extraneous variables are randomization, matching, homogeneous samples, and statistical control. The independent variable is the walking program and the dependent variable is blood glucose.

A is wrong: The independent variable is the walking program being tested.

B is wrong: The dependent variable is blood glucose.

D is wrong: Insulin use is being controlled because it could affect results, not just listed to describe the sample.

121. A nurse uses grounded theory to study how newly graduated nurses cope with their first year. She keeps interviewing new participants until no new themes or categories emerge. This point is called:

A. Triangulation

B. Randomization

C. Bracketing

D. Data saturation

Answer: D. Data saturation

Data saturation is the point in qualitative data collection when new interviews no longer produce new themes, categories or information, and it is the usual signal to stop sampling. This is why qualitative sample sizes are not fixed in advance as they are in quantitative studies. Grounded theory, phenomenology and ethnography all rely on this principle. Do not confuse it with bracketing, which is setting aside the researcher's own beliefs, or triangulation, which is the use of multiple methods, sources or investigators to strengthen findings.

A is wrong: Triangulation is combining more than one research strategy.

B is wrong: Randomization is a feature of probability sampling and experiments.

C is wrong: Bracketing is setting aside the researcher's own beliefs.

122. Before interviewing mothers of children with autism, a nurse researcher who herself has an autistic son writes down and deliberately sets aside her own beliefs and experiences so these do not color her interpretation. This is called:

A. Member checking

B. Bracketing

C. Saturation

D. Purposive sampling

Answer: B. Bracketing

Bracketing is the deliberate setting aside of the researcher's own beliefs, assumptions and experiences so they do not influence how participants' descriptions are collected and interpreted. It is especially associated with phenomenology, where the goal is to capture the lived experience of participants as they perceive it. A researcher with personal experience of the topic should document her biases in advance, often in a reflexive journal. Member checking, by comparison, happens after analysis and involves returning findings to participants to verify them.

A is wrong: Member checking is returning findings to participants to verify them.

C is wrong: Saturation is the point where no new information emerges.

D is wrong: Purposive sampling is a method of selecting participants.

123. After analyzing interviews with cancer survivors, a nurse researcher returns to the participants and asks them whether her summarized themes accurately reflect their experiences. This technique MAINLY strengthens the:

A. Credibility of qualitative findings

B. Statistical power of the study

C. Internal consistency reliability of a scale

D. Randomization of the sample

Answer: A. Credibility of qualitative findings

Member checking, or participant validation, means returning the interpreted findings to participants to confirm that they accurately reflect their experiences, and it strengthens the credibility of qualitative findings. Credibility is one of the criteria for trustworthiness in qualitative research, along with transferability, dependability and confirmability (Lincoln and Guba). Other strategies include prolonged engagement, triangulation, peer debriefing and an audit trail. Statistical power, internal consistency and randomization are quantitative concepts and do not apply here.

B is wrong: Statistical power applies to quantitative hypothesis testing.

C is wrong: Internal consistency applies to multi-item scales.

D is wrong: Randomization is unrelated to verifying interpretations.

124. Which research question is BEST suited to a QUALITATIVE design?

A. What are the typical behaviors and beliefs of Badjao mothers regarding childbirth?

B. Which antiseptic is more effective in preventing surgical site infection?

C. What factors are associated with low birth weight in a province?

D. What causes the increase in dengue cases during the rainy season?

Answer: A. What are the typical behaviors and beliefs of Badjao mothers regarding childbirth?

Qualitative questions explore the experiences, meanings, beliefs and typical behaviors of people or cultural groups, such as how Badjao mothers view childbirth, and they are answered with narrative data from interviews and observation. Quantitative questions deal with measurable variables, such as comparing the effectiveness of treatments, identifying factors associated with an outcome, or determining causes and effects. Exam tip: qualitative questions often start with what is the experience or how do they perceive, while quantitative ones ask which is more effective, how many, or what is the relationship.

B is wrong: Comparing treatment effectiveness is a quantitative question.

C is wrong: Factors associated with an outcome are studied quantitatively.

D is wrong: Questions about causes are quantitative.

125. A nurse wants to answer the question, "Which is more effective in reducing fever among children, tepid sponge bath or paracetamol alone?" This type of question calls for which approach?

A. Quantitative, experimental

B. Qualitative, phenomenological

C. Qualitative, ethnographic

D. Historical

Answer: A. Quantitative, experimental

A question asking which of two interventions is more effective compares treatments and outcomes, so it is quantitative and best answered with an experimental design in which the researcher manipulates the intervention and measures fever reduction. Qualitative designs address meaning and experience, such as phenomenology for lived experience and ethnography for culture. Historical research studies past events using records and documents. Memory aid: cause and effect or which is better means experimental, lived experience means phenomenology, culture means ethnography.

B is wrong: Phenomenology describes lived experience, not treatment effectiveness.

C is wrong: Ethnography describes culture.

D is wrong: Historical research examines past events.

126. A community health nurse tests a nutrition program in two schools. Because school officials will not allow random assignment, one school receives the program and the other does not. What is the main ADVANTAGE of this design?

A. It provides the most control over extraneous variables

B. It completely eliminates selection bias

C. It more closely approximates real-world conditions

D. It is the most prestigious design available

Answer: C. It more closely approximates real-world conditions

Quasi-experimental designs involve manipulation of an intervention but lack random assignment, which makes them practical in real settings such as schools and communities. Their advantage is that they more closely approximate the real world and are more feasible, but the disadvantage is less control over extraneous variables and a risk of selection bias. True experiments offer the most control through randomization, a control group and manipulation. The Solomon four-group design is considered the most rigorous experimental design.

A is wrong: Quasi-experiments offer less control than true experiments.

B is wrong: Without randomization, selection bias remains possible.

D is wrong: The Solomon four-group design is considered the most prestigious.

127. Why is the pre-experimental design considered the WEAKEST?

A. It always uses random assignment

B. The researcher has little control and threats to internal validity are not controlled

C. It requires four groups

D. It can only be used in qualitative research

Answer: B. The researcher has little control and threats to internal validity are not controlled

The pre-experimental design is considered the weakest because the researcher exercises little control and does not control threats to internal validity, so cause and effect cannot be established with confidence. Examples are the one-shot case study and the one-group pretest-posttest design. They lack randomization and often lack a comparison group. They are still quantitative and are sometimes used for exploratory purposes. Order of strength: pre-experimental, then quasi-experimental, then true experimental.

A is wrong: Random assignment is a feature of true experiments, not pre-experiments.

C is wrong: Four groups describe the Solomon design.

D is wrong: Pre-experimental designs are quantitative.

128. Clients are randomly assigned to two groups. Both groups have their anxiety measured before surgery, the experimental group listens to guided imagery while the other receives routine care, and both are measured again afterward. This design is the:

A. Posttest-only control group design

B. Solomon four-group design

C. One-shot case study

D. Pretest-posttest control group design

Answer: D. Pretest-posttest control group design

The pretest-posttest control group design is a true experiment with random assignment, a pretest for both groups, a treatment given only to the experimental group, and a posttest for both groups. The pretest allows the researcher to confirm group equivalence and to measure change. A posttest-only design omits the pretest, a Solomon design adds two more groups, and a one-shot case study has only one group measured once. Key words to watch: randomly assigned, both measured before and after, and treatment to one group only.

A is wrong: The posttest-only design has no pretest.

B is wrong: The Solomon design uses four groups.

C is wrong: A one-shot case study has a single group and no pretest or comparison.

129. A researcher fears that answering a pretest about breast self-examination would itself teach the women the topic. She randomly assigns women to two groups, gives only the experimental group the teaching, and measures both groups once at the end. This design is the:

A. Pretest-posttest control group design

B. Posttest-only control group design

C. Quasi-experimental nonequivalent group design

D. Cross-sectional survey

Answer: B. Posttest-only control group design

The posttest-only control group design is a true experiment in which participants are randomly assigned to groups, only the experimental group receives the treatment, and both groups are measured only once after the treatment. It is useful when a pretest might sensitize participants, such as when answering questions on breast self-examination already teaches the topic. Randomization is assumed to make the groups equivalent at the start. A pretest-posttest design would risk the testing effect described in this situation.

A is wrong: This design has no pretest.

C is wrong: There is random assignment, so it is not quasi-experimental.

D is wrong: There is manipulation of a treatment, so it is not a survey.

130. In a Solomon four-group design, how many of the four groups receive the pretest?

A. One

B. Two

C. Three

D. Four

Answer: B. Two

In the Solomon four-group design, only experimental group 1 and comparison group 1 receive the pretest, so exactly two of the four groups are pretested. The other two groups are posttested only. This arrangement allows the researcher to isolate the effect of the pretest itself from the effect of the treatment, which controls the testing threat. It combines the pretest-posttest and posttest-only control group designs, and it is considered the most rigorous experimental design, though it needs larger samples and more resources.

A is wrong: One group pretested would not allow comparison of pretest effects within both treated and untreated groups.

C is wrong: Only two of the four groups are pretested.

D is wrong: If all four were pretested, the pretest effect could not be isolated.

131. A researcher conducts a survey on the vaccine hesitancy of parents in a city. According to the handout, the control the researcher exercises in survey research lies mainly in the:

A. Sampling technique

B. Manipulation of the independent variable

C. Random assignment to treatment groups

D. Use of a placebo

Answer: A. Sampling technique
